Jean Gerson <note>A famous French theologian (1363–1429) and Chancellor of the University of Paris</note>, in his *Treatise on Errors Regarding the Magical Art* at the end of Part 1, narrates that good faith can destroy the works of the devil and proves it by an example, saying: Thus acted Philip <note>original: "Philippus," likely Philip IV of France, known as "the Fair"</note>, a certain King of the French, regarding a certain wax image which they said had been baptized and fashioned in his name in such a way that if it were destroyed, the King himself would die. And the pious King said, "We shall see, faithful servants, if God will be more powerful to destroy me than God is to save." And this, he says, our faith offers against the wicked.

Therefore, in the same place, he says <unclear>Amida</unclear> speaks of obedience to God, nor does he <unclear>spend</unclear>, <gloss>and of pilgrimage</gloss> <unclear>the first</unclear> many and <unclear>proclaiming</unclear> <gloss>of pilgrimage</gloss> as he attends <unclear>it may be a resonance</unclear>, thus <unclear>each testimony</unclear> as if someone who had been just, and as if he himself who had not been turned away from his God; so let him return to the prayers of God with his petitions, and he is turned about, liable to destruction. And of those whom <unclear>Christ</unclear> speaks of in Matthew 15: <note>original: "populus hic labiis me honorat, cor etiam..."</note> "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart" <note>Matthew 15:8</note> is not found there, so that it might more truly be said: "They blaspheme." Such is our diabolical obstinacy, but let us give these beans to divine providence <note>A colloquialism for leaving matters to God</note>, those who rather suffer rejection, not achieving the reward of divine <gloss>mercy</gloss> <unclear>imparted</unclear> by the counsel placed in Judith, chapter 8: <note>Judith 8:11–17</note> "We who have failed entirely before the Lord in every creature; why shall we not endure the scourges of a pious father?" We are children: we ought not, through impatience, to kick against the divine goad. <note>A reference to "kicking against the pricks" or the goad used for oxen</note>

***

Thérouanne <note>original: "Tervana," an ancient city in northern France</note>, a most ancient city of the Morini, was captured by the army of Charles V <note>The Holy Roman Emperor</note> on the 20th day of June 1553, and was utterly destroyed.

The sect of the Anabaptists <note>A radical Reformation movement</note> took its origin in 1525 in Germany from the Lutherans. When they had come in great numbers into the aforementioned country, they began to act maliciously in various regions against: Bishops, members of Religious Orders, and Monks; destroying castles and Monasteries, taking and plundering sacred vessels, chalices, and sacred vestments, treating them poorly. They exhibited no reverence to the venerable sacred <unclear>mysteries</unclear>; they abused virgins dedicated to God, and they tore up Missals and Ecclesiastical books, using them for their own <unclear>divine services</unclear>. For they were slaughtered in many and various places by the most Illustrious Duke of Lorraine, Antoine. <note>Antoine the Good (1489–1544), who famously suppressed the Peasants' War, which the author here associates with the Anabaptists</note>

*SINCE MANY OUTSTANDING
works by great craftsmen have this peculiar
quality: that they ennoble with famous celebrity
not only their own authors (to whose labor
and talent they owe the beginnings of their origin), but
also all those who have contributed some portion of their industry—whether in restoring damaged works to their former integrity or in polishing those covered in grime—or those to whom they were dedicated. Then, truly, from those monuments which bring some notable utility to the lives of mortals, true glory and fame of name usually fall to the illustrious craftsmen. For however great those works of excellent craftsmen may be, prepared either for the display of wealth and magnificence or for the show of talent, time nevertheless eventually consumes them all, disturbed from their state and dignity, so that besides the memory of the thing, not even ruins remain. # DEDICATION

->E P I S T O L A<-
<note>original: "Epistola" — Letter or Epistle</note>

* 3

building, adorning, and enlarging them, <note>original: "candis, ornandis, amplificandisq́," completing the words from the previous page</note> antiquity spared no superstitious expense. Even if they indeed delight us as miracles of art and talent, they nevertheless provide no practical use; they produce fame for their authors rather than true glory. However, they have earned more true praise who, by constructing bridges, baths, and aqueducts, have joined utility with the magnificence of their works. 

Among all these, however, the palm of victory—and deservedly so—is owed to those who have either left behind distinguished monuments of learning and talent that benefit the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>original: "Reipub. litterariæ" — the international community of scholars and the collective body of human knowledge</note>, or who have devoted useful effort to preserving the writings of good authors for posterity. 

For who would not admire the singular prudence of Gaius Julius Caesar—that greatest of monarchs and most powerful conqueror of almost the entire world? Who would not celebrate with a grateful heart and the highest praise his remarkable generosity? In calculating the year to align with the Sun <note>The reform of the Roman calendar into the Julian calendar</note>—a system we still use today—he employed the work of <term>Sosigenes the Mathematician</term> <note>An astronomer from Alexandria consulted by Caesar to design the Julian calendar</note> to establish it. 

The Egyptians may indeed extol to the heavens the excessive extravagances of their kings and the immense height of the Pyramids; yet this achievement of Caesar's will leave their fame far behind. I speak not of the glory of his own great deeds, but of that which he gained from this description of the year to its exact fullness, the distinction of days and months, and the restoration of the solstice and equinox points <note>original: "punctorum tropicorum" — the turning points of the sun</note> to their proper places. For in contracts, in legal judgments, in work both rural and domestic, and finally in the continuation of our studies and all other actions, we can in no way do without the clear distinction of time. Indeed, by this most ample benefit...

->E P I S T O L A<-

...benefit, it must be confessed that the entire world remains forever indebted to Caesar’s legacy <note>literally "ashes"</note>. The Carians may boast with immense praise of the most sumptuous tomb of their King <note>The Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note>; and in this matter, let the sign of Artemisia’s sincere love for her husband be no less celebrated. Yet, the piety of Augustus Caesar toward all posterity deserves greater praise, because he passed down to future generations that divine work of Virgil <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, the Roman poet</note>, which by the author’s own will was to be burned. Interposing his imperial authority, Augustus spoke with a noble voice truly worthy of an Emperor: *May the Muse of the divine Virgil live forever.* 

But truly, among others whose fame for learning and knowledge has reached celebrity, our Jacquier <note>Nicolas Jacquier (d. 1472), a Dominican inquisitor and author of this treatise</note> is not undeservedly counted by learned men. His work, which he titled ***The Scourge of Heretical Sorcerers*** <note>original: "Flagellum Haereticorum fascinariorum"</note>, is a living and breathing monument of his excellent talent. It has been kept in our library for over a hundred years until now, but I have not hesitated to commit it to the printing press and make it public because of the wonderful example of erudition it presents, and its very great utility for both common life and the Church of God. 

For, as Job truly says, <margin>Job 7</margin> *the life of man upon earth is a warfare*, in which the pious struggle at every moment against the weakness of their own flesh, against the allurements and terrors of the world, and finally—and most of all—against the enemy of God and men: the Devil and his instruments <note>original: "organis," referring to those who act as tools or agents of the devil, such as sorcerers</note>. Therefore, it is necessary not only that individual believers be equipped with the weapons necessary for the conflict, but most especially that the **watchmen of Israel** <note>A biblical term for the clergy or spiritual leaders, derived from Ezekiel</note>, to whom the care of the Church is divinely entrusted, be strengthened with prudence and practical experience, so that they might protect the citizens subject to them from the assaults...

<summary>Mintzenburg compares the preservation of Jacquier’s manuscript to Augustus saving Virgil’s Aeneid, arguing that the book is a vital weapon for the Church in the spiritual warfare against the Devil and sorcery.</summary>

### DEDICATORY.

<sig>* 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: from</meta>

...from the most violent assaults of that enemy, they might be kept safe. And just as it is the duty of a good general, and one skilled in military affairs, not only to be concerned about provisions, to select a suitable site for the camp, to exhort the soldiers to battle, and to add courage to the fearful; but most of all, to strive so that the army receives no harm—so far as that is possible—and that the battle is engaged with the least risk: so our Jacquier here, having been trained for a long time and to a great extent, not in this military arena but in that spiritual *palæstra* <note>original: "palæstra" — a Greek term for a wrestling school or place of exercise; here used metaphorically for spiritual training</note>, performing the duty of a good general in this little book, having exposed the principal snares and delusions of the Devil himself and of his tools, the sorcerers, demonstrates by the examples of the Fathers how the blows of the enemy are either to be avoided, or if you cannot avoid them, how they are to be received; likewise, he shows the manner and method of restraining heretical sorcerers. This gift would have been lost to us, had it not been preserved by some fate, or rather by divine providence, and rescued from the injury of moths and time, proving by its own example, fact, and outcome that which was truly said in the verse:

->*That it may live, a book must have a Genius.*<-
<note>original: "Ut vivat Genium debet habere liber." A 'Genius' refers to an inherent spark of life or a protective spirit that ensures a work's longevity.</note>

There is no doubt, therefore, that the use of this most profitable little book has been granted to us by divine power. And lest we seem ungrateful toward the majesty of the Divine <note>original: "Numinis" — the divine will or power of God</note>, we thought that this offered opportunity should be seized, the little book itself dragged out from the darkness and given light, and that it should be made to be reborn, as it were, into the world from its almost lamented ruins.

**from** *the best authors of our own and the previous age, collected so that the reading of this* author, *by comparison with others, might be more enlightened, and also more pleasing by the variety of short works; -> ### DEDICATORY [EPISTLE] <-

<center>D E D I C A T O R Y.</center>

* s 5

...no two things involve more business. The same can be seriously and truly said: that work will never be lacking for him who wishes to undertake the task of restoring **Jaquier** <note>Nicolas Jaquier (d. 1472), a Dominican inquisitor and author of the *Flagellum Haereticorum Fascinariorum* (Scourge of Heretical Witches)</note>. For even if there were no other cause, the carelessness of certain scribes certainly ensures that, even among the most approved writers, learned men must always re-weave, so to speak, **Penelope’s web** <note>original: "tela Penelopes" — a reference to the web woven by Penelope in Homer's Odyssey, which she unwove every night to delay her suitors; here it signifies a task that must be constantly redone because others continually undo the progress</note>, since those same **Printers** <note>original: "Typographi"</note> daily corrupt more by their **indolence** <note>original: "socordia"</note> than the diligence of the learned can restore.

Some works possessed such divine quality that they deterred the hands of all craftsmen, by an inimitable excellence of art, either from completing what was **begun** <note>original: "inchoatum"</note> or from mending what was corrupted. Among the works of **Apelles** <note>The most famous painter of ancient Greece, active in the 4th century BCE</note>, two **Venuses** are especially celebrated by writers: one emerging from the sea, and the other which he began at Cos, intended even to surpass the former, had not death envied the work as it was being born. No one was found who could repair the damaged lower part of the former, and no one could finish the latter according to the prescribed outlines.

Just as the modesty of these ancient artists is to be praised, so the negligence of those men is the more gravely to be detested who have so corrupted the work of **Jaquier**—which should be placed before all the statues of all sculptors and the paintings of all artists—by their copying, that they seem to have conspired with minds devoted to the destruction of such an eminent author. And so that this evil might not gradually creep further, it ought to be the concern of learned men, since there is hardly any book more worthy of being worn out in the hands of students, because from no other can a knowledge of many things be more quickly drawn. What, however, more becomes learned men than to excel others, as in piety, so in pru-

<meta>This page continues Johann Mintzenburg’s dedicatory epistle. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing the difficulty of repairing damaged works of art and literature. This page begins by completing the word "Prudence" [Prudentia], continuing the philosophical argument that wisdom gained through experience alone is often too costly or arrives too late for the urgent needs of the State.</meta>

-> ### E P I S T L E <-

*...dence excel? Truly, Prudence, which is gathered from the long use of things, is not only wretched—as that man truly wrote—because it is prepared at the great misfortune of many, but it is also costly, so that it usually arrives too late. But the **State** <term>Respublica — the "public thing" or common good</term> no more tolerates these delays than a ship in danger at sea tolerates an unskilled pilot until he becomes proficient; for immediate danger requires a craftsman who is already prepared. Therefore, there is no leisure to lose any portion of life, nor is it permitted to be boys; a **maturity of mind** <note>original: "animi canicies" — literally "a greyness of the mind," meaning wisdom or maturity that precedes physical aging</note> ought to be present, and this is gathered no more correctly from anywhere else than from this work. But, to proceed with what I began: the more detestable the rashness of those who corrupt texts is, the more all learned men, each according to his strength and with greater religious devotion, ought to apply their hand to restoring the work. Indeed, it is **superstition** <note>In this context, a misplaced or paralyzing reverence for old, corrupted texts</note> to dare nothing here, since such daring has turned out most happily for so many. It is **rashness** <term>temeritas</term> to replace the new after having deleted the old writing based on any slight conjecture. Yet it is a mark of **integrity** <note>original: "candoris" — literally "brightness" or "whiteness," referring to the purity and honesty of a scholar's intentions</note> to note separately if anything has been discovered through probable arguments, and to lay a foundation, as it were, for the learned to investigate further. And would that all the **Leaders** <term>Proceres — the elite or "princes" of the Republic of Letters</term> of the literary world would unite in this most beautiful business, so that each might contribute what he has discovered to the common good, until we might have the study of letters perfected. No light reward is offered; even one restored passage will earn an honorable memory of one's name among scholars.*

*In this work, truly, such care has been taken that, at my own risk, I do not hesitate to promise that never until now has **Jaquier** <note>Referring to the text of Nicolas Jaquier's "Flagellum Haereticorum Fascinariorum"</note> been seen more successfully handled. As for what remains,*

-> # D E D I C A T O R Y <-

...character of the editor] is, I hope, that an impartial judge of things may fall to my lot—one who weighs our study, faith, and goodwill more than he weaves a slander or drags all our words and deeds into the worst possible light, should any human error happen to occur by chance. Let all those who wish well for the world of literature take an example from us; by looking out for the public good with kindness, may they support this most honorable and, for human affairs, extremely necessary kind of study. By doing so, they will earn immortal gratitude not only from me, but from all good men.

To you indeed, Reverend Sir, it has pleased me to offer this edition of **Jaquerius** <term>Nicolas Jaquerius (d. 1472), a Dominican inquisitor and author of works defending the reality of witchcraft</term> and to consecrate it to your name. My hope is that, as it now emerges into the light for the first time, it might be safe under your patronage against the venomous bites of **Sycophants** <note>original: "Sycophantarum" — here meaning malicious critics or slanderers who attack the work of others</note> through the authority of Your Reverence. 

For such is the **religious piety** <note>original: "religiosa pietas"</note> of your Reverend dignity, such is your knowledge of divine and human affairs, and such is your faith and prudence in managing business—and finally, your justice toward everyone, joined with a singular benevolence—that you were appointed **Prefect of the Treasury** <term>ærarij Præfectus — the official overseer of the community's finances or public funds</term>. This appointment came by the unanimous choice of your entire assembly, with the united votes of everyone and the great applause of all good men, and certainly not without the favor of the Divine Power. 

Indeed, your services and the honors you have bestowed upon me, and even upon our entire Order, are so great and so many that it would be an endless task to recount even the least of them. Therefore, it was only right that, to declare my gratitude in return, I should dedicate the edition of these treatises contained in this present book to Your Reverence—the one man among all who is most conspicuous for every kind of virtue.

This will be all the more pleasing to me because I have found such a Judge—one who not only outshines many others by the testimony of his solid learning, uncommon prudence, and distinguished modesty, but also one who is proven to be powerful in the management of various affairs. This is witnessed by that most noble **Arnsburg Monastery** <term>Arnspurgense Monasterium — Arnsburg Abbey, a prominent Cistercian monastery in Hesse, Germany</term>, in the administration of which you have successfully served for several years with much praise, and indeed continue to serve.

Furthermore, you will ensure that one day, God willing, I may bring forth other excellent works into public view, so that our study may be daily increased, and the kindness of **God and our Savior** <note>original: "DEI & Seruatoris nostri"</note> may be proclaimed by all.

# A SCOURGE
## OF HERETICS

->*OF SORCERERS, BY THE AUTHOR BROTHER*<-
->*Nicolas Jaquier, of the Order of Preachers* <term>Ordinis fratrum Prædicatorum — Commonly known as the Dominicans, an order of monks focused on preaching and combating heresy through education.</term>*, and formerly Inquisitor of Heretical*<-
->*Depravity* <term>Inquiſitore Hæreticæ prauitatis — An official authorized by the Church to investigate and suppress beliefs or practices that contradicted established Catholic doctrine.</term>*, etc.*<-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut drop-cap 'F' featuring ornate foliate scrolls and a small humanoid face integrated into the design.</image-desc>

The **Scourge of Sorcerers** <note>original: "Flagellvm Faſcinariorum" — The term "fascinarius" refers to one who bewitches or casts spells, which Jaquier equates with heresy.</note>, specifically of Heretics: compelled by the obstacles frequently occurring in the office of the Inquisition, I, Brother Nicolas Jaquier, a humble member of the **Order of Preachers**, have chosen to compose in a simple style—drawn from the divine scriptures and the doctrines of the saints—a "scourge" by which there may be cast out from the temple of God (which is the Church of the faithful) certain perverse dogmas and foolish assertions. Supported by these errors, many people are seen to offer excessive favors and disguised defenses to these heretical sorcerers, leading to the grave loss of the Catholic faith, the great prejudice of the lowly faithful, and a dangerous scandal. For just as the demons, the founders of this abominable sect, subvert men and convert them to this sect—the worst of all other heresies—so that through them they [the demons] might be wor- <note>The text ends mid-word on the Latin "colan-", likely leading to "colantur" (be worshipped).</note>

...might be worshipped. Therefore, many claim that the aforementioned **sorcerers** <note>original: "fascinarios" — those who cast spells or use "fascination," here used to mean witches.</note> are so deceived by the operation of the **Demon** through fantastic illusions in their sleep that, upon waking, they believe they have met together at night in certain places with one another and with Demons. They believe they have worshipped there, as if in a certain **synagogue** <note>original: "synagoga" — a term used by early inquisitors to describe what would later be called a "Sabbat" or gathering of witches.</note> of Demons, and honored the Demons themselves with offerings. They believe that at the suggestion of these same Demons, they denied **GOD** and the Catholic faith, performed many services for the Demons there, and accepted the promised help from them—even though, as the aforementioned claimants pretend, these events do not happen to the sorcerers in reality while they are awake, but only through the internal illusion of those who are sleeping.

To support this assertion of theirs, they cite as a parallel the narrative concerning certain women who were long ago so deluded by the operation of Demons that they believed they traveled across vast distances at night with **Diana** <note>The Roman goddess of the moon and hunting.</note> and **Herodias** <note>A biblical figure (wife of Herod), often associated in medieval folklore with Diana as a leader of the "night-raid" or "wild hunt."</note>, as is recounted in the book called the **Book of Decrees** <note>original: "Decretorum liber" — specifically the *Decretum Gratiani*, a 12th-century collection of Canon Law.</note>, in a certain chapter beginning with the word: "**Episcopi**" <note>This refers to the *Canon Episcopi*, a vital legal text that skeptical theologians used to argue that the flight of witches was an illusion, not a physical reality.</note>, in Question 5 of the 26th Case. ### P R E F A C E

...judged <note>The text picks up from the previous page's argument about what skeptics believe should be believed or judged.</note> that **Demons** do not have, nor has such great power been granted to them, to perpetrate so many and such great **evil deeds** <note>original: "maleficia" — specifically harmful magic or "witchcraft" intended to cause physical or material damage.</note> at the invocation of their worshippers, the **sorcerers** <note>original: "fascinariorum" — literally "those who fascinate" or cast spells with the eyes, a common term for witches in this period.</note>, as these very sorcerers confess are done through the patronage of the Demons whom they worship. 

For it seems strange to many, as they assert, and therefore highly incredible to them, that the supremely good and almighty **God** would give or permit the **Demons**—enemies of humanity and rejected by God Himself—so much power over fragile humans as to harass them with such great and serious evil acts. They argue this is done not only to people's bodies, by inflicting illnesses, weaknesses, fits of madness, deaths, and almost countless torments, but also through the destruction of the external goods granted for human use. 

Furthermore, they think they have made a powerful point <note>original: "magnum aliquid intonuisse" — literally "thundered something great."</note> when they add: that if Demons had such great power over humans and their external possessions, they would quickly exterminate all people and consume their goods, since they are the implacable enemies of mankind. Because the Demons do not do this—and yet the perverse will of these same demons is certainly not lacking—the skeptics strive to conclude that the **power** <note>original: "potestas"</note> to do so is not in them. They also strive to maintain that, in the legal process and punishment of sorcerers caught in this specific crime of heresy, no distinction should be made between them and other heretics who are found to have deviated from the faith merely through some erroneous opinion or assertion. Many people daily bring forward these and similar inventions to fuel the heresy and sect of the sorcerers <note>original: "fascinariorum" — derived from "fascination" or the evil eye; Jaquier uses this specifically to describe the "new" sect of witches emerging in the 15th century</note> and to hinder its extirpation. 

Therefore, desiring to contribute my effort, according to my modest ability, to the cause of the sacred faith—which has been excessively disturbed by this heresy and the worst of sects—and trusting in the help of the Most High, I have undertaken this Little Work <note>original: "Opusculum" — a common self-deprecating term used by authors for their books</note>. I have taken care to divide it into certain sections, as if into specific chapters, from which, like various cords made and woven together, there may result a **Scourge of Sorcerers** <note>original: "Flagellum fascinariorum" — the title of the book; the author is literally saying his chapters are the "cords" of a whip used to punish heretics</note>.

# WHAT IT IS TO **MOCK** AND IN **WHAT**
# **VARIOUS WAYS**
## *it is understood.*

### CHAPTER ONE.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated drop cap 'Q' featuring a central grotesque mask or face surrounded by elaborate foliate scrolls and vines.</image-desc>

SINCE, therefore, it is necessary to speak of **illusions** <note>The Latin *illusio* carries a dual meaning: it can refer to a deceptive "illusion" or "trickery," but also to "mockery" or "derision." The author explores both senses here.</note>, we must first see what an illusion is. Wherefore it must be considered that in the Holy Scriptures, "Illusion" sometimes signifies **mockery** <note>original: "derisionem"</note>, which is a sin by which a neighbor is unjustly despised. This is as Herod did to Christ, as written in the 23rd chapter of Luke, where it is said: *But Herod with his army despised him and mocked him, and having clothed him in a white robe, sent him back to Pilate.* <note>original: "Spreuit autem illum Herodes cum exercitu fuo, & illufit, indutumque vefte alba remifit ad Pilatum." See Luke 23:11.</note>

In another way, however, illusion is understood as a **deliberate representation** by which one wishes to hide their true intent by veiling it. This kind of illusion is sometimes done for a good purpose, and without harm to the person who is deceived. For in this way, Michal, the daughter of King Saul and wife of David, deceived her father when he wanted to kill her husband David. She herself let David down through a window from...

# ON FALSE REPRESENTATIONS
## *which Demons sometimes bring about for sleeping people, mocking them through internal phantoms.*

### CHAPTER TWO.

It frequently happens to sleeping people that representations of certain things are created within them, which they then believe they are doing, even though they do not actually do them; or they believe they possess things they do not have, but are merely dreaming. Holy Scripture also testifies to this, using the deception of dreamers to clarify a point, describing the likeness of a dreamer by saying:

> Just as the hungry man dreams and eats, but when he has woken up his soul is empty; and just as the thirsty man dreams and drinks, and when he has woken up he is still weary and thirsty, and his soul is empty, so shall be the multitude of all the nations that fought against Mount Zion.

Isaiah, chapter 29. Moreover, apparitions of this kind occur in sleepers through the descent of abundant blood to the sensory source <note>original: *principium sensitivum*. Therefore, the Devil appeared to Christ perceptibly, not only according to the sense of sight, but also to the sense of hearing, by speaking the aforementioned words to him. Similarly, he also appeared to the sense of touch, because he took him up to a very high mountain, showing him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. 

In this same way, it is very frequently read that Demons appeared perceptibly to many saints through the external senses, both in human form or likeness and in the form of various beasts. Martin replied: "The Lord is my helper, I will not fear what man can do to me," and immediately that one vanished.

# ON THE THREE WAYS IN WHICH
## **Demons Manifest to the Senses**

**There** are three ways in which **Demons** are accustomed to present themselves to the external senses <note>In medieval scholastic philosophy, "exterior senses" refers to the five physical senses (sight, hearing, etc.), while "interior senses" refers to things like imagination and memory.</note> of human beings. In the **first way**, they act through some physical thing produced by God or by nature; the Demons, with God’s permission, take hold of this thing so that they may use it as a medium to do or say something to people. 

In this manner, the **Devil** spoke through the serpent (which was created by God) to **Eve**, and deceived her, leading her to transgress the divine command by eating the forbidden fruit, as seen in **Genesis, chapter 3**. 

In this same way, the Devil spoke to people through a certain young girl by means of divination <note>original: *divinando* — the act of foretelling the future or revealing hidden knowledge through supernatural means.</note>. She brought great profit to her masters through this, and it was through this girl that the Devil himself praised the **Apostle Paul**, **Silas**, and **Luke** in their presence. Paul cast this Devil out from the girl in the name of Christ, as recorded in **Acts, chapter 16**, where it is said:

> "Now it happened, as we were going to prayer, that a certain girl having a spirit of divination <note>original: *spiritum pythonem* — literally a "pythian spirit." This term refers back to the Oracle of Delphi in Greece, where the priestess of Apollo was called the Pythia; here, the biblical text uses it to describe a demonic spirit of prophecy.</note> met us, who brought her masters much profit by fortune-telling. This girl followed Paul and us, crying out, 'These men are the servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us the way of salvation!'"

Through this same method, Demons have frequently spoken

In the **second way**, however, **Demons** sometimes present themselves to the external senses of certain people through objects made by human skill for the worship and invocation of those same Demons—such as **idols** manufactured for the service of Demons. In these objects, Demons sometimes dwell and give answers to their worshipers, as is evident in the legends of the **Saints**: **Bartholomew**, **Simon and Jude**, and very many other saints <note>The "Golden Legend" and other medieval hagiographies frequently describe saints confronting demons who lived inside statues and spoke to pagan priests.</note>.

In this way also, **Necromancers** <note>original: *Nigromantici* — literally "black-diviners," those who practice magic involving the dead or demons.</note> and practitioners of the **magical arts** fashion images and rings, and other such things with superstitious observances subtly devised by Demons for the deception of men and for the worship of the Demons themselves. **C**onsideration must be given, however, to the fact that although the bodies formed and assumed by **Demons** are perceptible to the external senses of humans, they are not actually living bodies. Indeed, the soul performs two functions in its own body: first, it vivifies it, and for this reason, the soul is called the <term>form of the body</term><note>original: *forma corporis*—a concept from Aristotelian philosophy used by medieval theologians. It means the soul is the "organizing principle" that makes a body a living person rather than just a lump of matter.</note>, because it grants it life. Second, the soul moves the body and its limbs. 

It is not the same, however, regarding the soul in relation to the **clothing** with which a body is dressed; for although the soul may move the clothing, it does not give life to the garment, but merely moves it, just as a **sailor** moves a ship but does not give it life. 

In this way, **Demons** use the bodies they have formed, moving them and operating through them among humans; within these bodies, they form voices and intelligible words, and through them perform actions similar to the functions of life, even though bodies of this sort are not alive. Consequently, as soon as the **Demons** abandon them, they dissolve and vanish back into their <term>original matter</term><note>original: *materiam pristinam*—the raw elemental substance, such as thickened air or dust, from which the demon temporarily constructed the form.</note> from which they were fashioned.

Certain people, by incautiously and dangerously focusing on the chapter **Episcopi** <note>original: "c. Episcopi." The *Canon Episcopi* was a 10th-century legal text incorporated into canon law. It claimed that women who believed they rode through the night with the goddess Diana were victims of demonic illusions. Sceptics used it to argue that witchcraft wasn't real, which Jacquier seeks to debunk.</note>, present no small obstacle to the extirpation of the sect and heresy of **witches** <term>fascinariorum: specifically those who use "fascination" or the evil eye; Jacquier uses it to describe the "new" sect of heretical witches</term>, through which this heresy receives favor and growth. Therefore, it seems necessary to say something both regarding the authority of this chapter *Episcopi* and regarding its actual content.

Regarding its authority, it must be asked by whom the said chapter *Episcopi* was produced. For **Gratian** <note>Johannes Gratian (d. 1159), the jurist who compiled the *Decretum*, the most important collection of canon law in the Middle Ages.</note> asserts that it was taken from the **Council of Ancyra** <note>original: "concilio Acquirensi." This is a common medieval misspelling/corruption of the Council of Ancyra (314 AD). Jacquier is undermining the text by pointing out its local, rather than global, origin.</note>. However, that Council of Ancyra was not among the general or universal councils, but was a certain particular council of some churchmen; for this reason, it does not possess the same authority as the general or universal councils, nor is it like the statutes or teachings of the **Supreme Pontiffs** <note>The Popes.</note> or the Holy Doctors of the Church.

Furthermore, Gratian took care to place the authors of those chapters at the head of each section of his book, which is called the **Decretum** <note>original: "Decretorum." The *Concordant of Discordant Canons*, the foundational textbook for medieval lawyers.</note>, so that the prudent reader might know how to discern and judge, or even weigh the authority of individual chapters; this is because not all sayings or chapters contained in that same book are of equal weight or authority. For they derive their weight of authority from their cited authors, placed by Gratian himself at the beginning of each chapter, from which also

<header>By Friar Nicholas Jacquier</header>

Now, certain chapters contained in the same book are called **chaff** <note>original: "paleę." In medieval canon law, *paleae* (literally "chaff" or "straw") referred to additions made to Gratian's *Decretum*. Therefore, the aforementioned chapter **Episcopi** is not of such great reputation as most other chapters of that same book, since it is evident from its very tenor that it was produced quite poorly, lightly, and crudely, as is clear from what follows.

For, to prove that the representation made to certain women—of whom the chapter speaks—was made only in their spirit (namely, in the internal imagination alone, and not by the physical experience of the external senses), it introduces two examples from Holy Scripture: namely, the Prophet Ezekiel and the Apostle Paul, saying:

"Who indeed would be so foolish and dull as to think that all these things, which happen only in the spirit, also happen in the body? For the Prophet Ezekiel saw and heard the visions of the Lord in the spirit, not in the body, just as he himself says: 'Immediately,' he says, 'I was in the spirit' <note>Ezekiel 1:1 and various passages. Jacquier is quoting the *Canon Episcopi* here, which uses Ezekiel’s spiritual visions to argue that witches only "ride with Diana" in their minds.</note>. And the Apostle Paul does not dare to say he was in the body, but says: 'Whether in the spirit, or out of the body, I do not know; God knows' <note>2 Corinthians 12:2. Paul describes being "caught up to the third heaven," but is unsure if it was a physical or purely spiritual experience.</note>."

However, whatever may be the case regarding the illusion made to women in the spirit alone—of which the aforementioned chapter *Episcopi* speaks—this is nevertheless not effectively proven by the example brought forward concerning Ezekiel,

-># The Scourge of the Bewitching Heretics<-

...who says he was in Jerusalem in spirit, in visions. For if Ezekiel was only in Jerusalem in spirit and in visions in such a way that he could not also have been there in the body, nor be **transferred bodily** <term>corporaliter: a physical, flesh-and-blood movement as opposed to a mental or spiritual vision</term> from Chaldea—where he was physically located at that time—then the proof which the said chapter **Episcopi** <note>The *Canon Episcopi* was a 10th-century legal text that claimed witchcraft was a delusion. Jacquier is trying to prove the Canon is wrong and that witches' flights are real physical events.</note> intends to make would be true: namely, that the aforementioned women were only in spirit and not in body during their visions, and that they were deceived in dreams.

But for this reason, the aforementioned proof is ineffective. For although Ezekiel was in the body in Chaldea when he was in Jerusalem in spirit through the visions of God, it could also easily have happened physically, such that he was not only in Jerusalem in spirit, but also present there in the body, having been carried and translated there.

This is just as we read concerning the Prophet **Habakkuk** <note>original: "Abacuc." This story is found in the deuterocanonical portion of the Book of Daniel (Bel and the Dragon), which was included in the Latin Vulgate Bible used by Jacquier.</note>, who by angelic power was **translated bodily** from Judea into Chaldea to Daniel in the lions' den, and was then returned from there back to Judea, as seen in **Daniel chapter 14**, where it is said:

"Now the Prophet Habakkuk was in Judea, and he had cooked a stew, and had broken bread into a bowl, and was going into the field to carry it to the harvesters. # Friar Nicholas Jaquier

...take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist in the evil day <note>original: "accipite armaturā Dei, vt poſsitis reſiſtere in die malo," quoting Ephesians 6:13</note>. Moreover, besides the various armors of spiritual virtues which the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> adds in that same place, there are also other armors given to the faithful by divine gift against the wickedness of the Devil. 

<margin>Armor. 1. Prayer.</margin>

One of these is a devout recourse to divine help; this recourse is made through various types of prayer, whether vocal <note>spoken aloud</note> or mental <note>silent, internal prayer</note>. For indeed, as David says, there are many mercies for all who call upon God <note>Psalm 86:5 (numbered as Psalm 80 in the Vulgate tradition mentioned here)</note>. Therefore, in the Lord’s Prayer, it is said, **"deliver us from evil,"** which is quite rightly understood to refer also to the malice of the Devil. 

It is not only necessary for the faithful to pray to GOD, but also to request that the prayers of the saints be offered before GOD—and especially those of the most blessed Virgin Mary, whose power and protection are effectively and uniquely potent for crushing the strength of the enemy. Hence, in her Hymn <note>The "Maria Mater Gratiae," a hymn traditionally used in the Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary</note> it is said: *Mary, mother of grace, mother of mercy, protect us from the enemy.* Likewise, it is frequently said in her Office <note>The "Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary," a standard set of daily prayers</note>: *Vouchsafe that I may praise you, sacred Virgin; give me strength against your enemies.* For the Demons are the enemies of the Mother of God, because through her the human race was liberated from their servitude—the same race that had been made subject to their servitude through Eve.

--- Page 151 ---
<meta>This page continues Nicolas Jacquier’s argument from page 110. While the previous page established that Guardian Angels protect humans from direct demonic assault, this page explains why demons recruit human "witches" or "evil-doers" to bypass those celestial defenses.</meta>

<page-num>113</page-num>
<header>Friar Nicolas Jacquier <note>Nicolas Jacquier (c. 1400–1472) was a French Dominican inquisitor and author of the *Flagellum Haereticorum Fascinariorum* (The Scourge of Heretical Witches), one of the earliest manuals on the persecution of witches.</note></header>

**D**emons use the service of their worshippers in their operations regarding humans for a two-fold reason. The first reason is indeed because, as is clear from the preceding sections, demons are hindered in many ways and frequently in the exercise of their power; they are prohibited or kept away from humans either by the ministry of Angels or by the other divine armors mentioned above. Consequently, what they cannot do by themselves, they sometimes accomplish through the service of their <term>evil-doing worshippers</term> <note>original: *maleficorum*, often translated as "witches" or "sorcerers" in this period.</note>, who can draw near to other people without difficulty and approach them more easily. To these evil-doers, the demons sometimes hand over poisoned substances to be secretly administered to the people they intend to harm. For all such evil-doers in common—and especially the <term>heretical witches</term> <note>original: *hæretici fascinarii*. Jacquier specifically links witchcraft to heresy, a key legal shift in the 15th century.</note>—are traitors and accustomed to deceptions in the perpetration of their evil deeds, so that they might not be hindered or caught. Along with this, they are for the most part the greatest hypocrites in both their words and their deeds.

The beggar **Lazarus** also died, and was carried by Angels into the bosom of **Abraham**. Luke, chapter 16.

Poverty and infirmity preserved **Lazarus**. It is no less a good thing that God preserves one from an imminent evil than that He relieves one from an oppressive evil. There was no less grace in **Paul**, whom God preserved from the exaltation of pride, than there was in **Peter**, whom He healed, preserved, and raised up from presumption because he had wrongly trusted in himself.

For **Paul** said of himself: "Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh <note>original: "stimulus carnis meæ"</note>, an Angel of Satan, to buffet me <note>original: "colaphizet," literally to strike with fists</note>." 2 Corinthians, chapter 12. This buffeting sent to **Paul** through an Angel of Satan was a very good thing, through which his humility was preserved unharmed, without which he could not be saved. ## THAT DIVINE WISDOM
### permits demons and their malevolent witch-worshippers <note>original: "fascinarios." Jacquier uses this term to describe a specific sect of heretical witches who, in his view, have entered a formal pact with the devil.</note> to commit many evil deeds <term>maleficia <gloss>harmful magic or crimes committed through demonic power</gloss></term> against humans, for the instruction of the faithful, even though both the witches and their evil deeds are displeasing to God.

### CHAPTER 24.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'E' featuring decorative scrollwork and a small face or mask integrated into the lower-left flourish.</image-desc>
Instruction arises from the operations and evil deeds <note>original: "maleficijs"</note> of demons and witches in three ways for those to whom such operations and evil deeds become known. The first instruction, indeed, concerns the constant malice and dangerous perversity of the demons, who are the enemies of human salvation. For just as if someone knows they have mortal enemies, they think of them more frequently and provide for their own safety more cautiously against them when they frequently perceive some of their efforts, works, machinations, or attacks being attempted against them, rather than if they perceived nothing of the sort for a long time. Therefore, when the Devil speaks "from his own," he is not to be believed, because he is a liar and a deceiver.

To these servants, according to the **Gospel** doctrine, God has given power over **Demons**; in such instances, the Devil does not speak from his own accord. 

For **God**, for His own glory, the exaltation of His faith, the edification of the faithful, and the confusion of the Devil himself, wisely and powerfully uses even perverse and <term>reprobate <gloss>Latin: "reprobis"—those rejected by God or beyond hope of salvation</term> men and malignant spirits to proclaim the <term>saving truth <gloss>Latin: "veritatem ſalutarem"</gloss></term>. 

Faith must be shown to this truth, not because of the nature of the men or the **Demons** who speak it, but because of **divine authority**. For in those moments, the Demons do not speak from their own nature, but as if compelled by <term>another’s power <gloss>Latin: "alienis compulſi"</gloss></term>—namely, by the power of God.

From the aforementioned points, it is clear that in every operation of a **Demon** concerning humans, a twofold power <term>potestas: here meaning the authority or the capacity to act</term> concurs. Specifically, there is the natural power of the **Demon**, which is indeed great, but it is bound by **God**, who mercifully looks after humans—beings whom the **Demons**, though naturally more powerful, treat as enemies. The other power is divine permission, without which the natural power of a **Demon** cannot be exercised against humans in this world.

For a **Demon** cannot perform any operation by his natural power concerning humans, except as often and as much as **God** permits—whose judgments, though they are incomprehensible, are nonetheless beyond reproach. For indeed, we read that when **Satan** desired to tempt **Job**, **God** gave him power, but not over **Job's** own person. For it is written that the **Lord** said to **Satan** himself:

<page-num>173</page-num>
<header>Friar Nicolas Jacquier</header>

...since there would be a great risk of expanding and multiplying this sect if one did not rely on the testimony of accomplices and participants, according to the ordinance made regarding this matter, as is found in the chapter *In favor of the faith* <note>original: "In fidei fauorem." If he further argues that **God** did indeed permit it, the answer is that the person making this allegation must sufficiently prove it and duly inform the **Judge** regarding it. Just as if someone were accused by thieves of having been with them during a theft on a certain day and at a certain place, and he alleges that he was elsewhere on that day and place—such that he could not have been with the thieves—unless he has sufficiently proven this, such an allegation or defense does not support him, nor does it benefit him. 

In the same way, one who says or alleges that a false **representation** was made of him by the **Demon** should not be believed unless he makes this fact clearly established; otherwise, he should be judged as a liar and a fabricator <note>original: "fictus & adinuentor"</note>.

<summary>Nicolas Jacquier argues that in witchcraft trials, the burden of proof for "spectral evidence" lies with the defendant. He uses a legal analogy to common theft to show that claiming a demon impersonated you is an empty defense unless it can be miraculously proven.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Nicolas Jacquier’s legal and theological argument from page 180. He is arguing that if "witch-heretics" are treated as ordinary heretics (who might be shown leniency if they repent), it would create a dangerous loophole. Criminals might join the "sect of witches" simply to commit murders and seek revenge more secretly, hoping for the lighter punishments sometimes offered by ecclesiastical courts compared to the harsh penalties of secular law.</meta>

<page-num>181</page-num>
<header>Brother Nicolas Jacquier</header>
<sig>M 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: THAT (original: QVOD)</meta>

because of the incentive toward this kind of **heresy of the witch-heretics** <note>original: *fascinariorum* — Jacquier’s specific term for those who combine magic with the "new" heresy of devil-worship</note>; for since perverse and impulsive men frequently refrain from committing crimes out of fear of the grave punishments they believe they would suffer for perpetrating such outrages, if they believed they would go unpunished, or at least be punished less severely, they would then be incited to commit evils. Therefore, if those who are perverse and inclined toward evil deeds—such as **murders and acts of revenge** <note>original: *homicidia & vindicatiões*</note>—and driven by passion, perceive that crimes committed through the medium of **heretical depravity** <term>hæreticæ prauitatis: the standard legal phrasing for the "wickedness" or "infection" of heresy within a community</term> and the sect of the witch-heretics are not punished as much, or are punished less than if they were committed without the crime of heresy, they would easily be incited to enter and embrace this most wicked sect. This is especially true since they could more easily and secretly fulfill their perverse desires by means of this corrupt heresy and sect. Therefore, it seems irrational and dangerous to open and affirm this path regarding this widespread sect, since it is not found that the Church intended for the aforementioned crimes to remain without worthy punishment simply because they were committed with heretical depravity and through its means and the **patronage of the Devil** <note>original: *Dæmonis patrocinio* — the concept that the Devil acts as a legal advocate or supernatural protector for his followers</note>, especially since they demand greater punishment precisely because they were committed through such a perverse medium of heretical depravity.

<summary>Jacquier argues that witch-heretics must be punished more severely than ordinary criminals or simple heretics to prevent the sect from becoming a "haven" for murderers seeking to escape secular justice. He claims that using demonic aid to commit crimes actually increases the severity of the offense.</summary>

## EVEN SUPPOSING THAT
## *witch-heretics were deluded by demons in their sleep just like the women mentioned in the chapter "Episcopi," they are nonetheless in no way excused from heretical depravity.*

### C H A P T E R  X X V I I I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a square woodcut border with ornate foliate and vine scrollwork.</image-desc>

Even assuming that this heretical sect of **witch-heretics** <note>original: *fascinariorum* — Jacquier’s term for this specific "new" sect of devil-worshipping witches</note> had its origin in a fantastic illusion caused by demons working internally upon the imagination—providing imaginary representations of demons to the witch-heretics, just as the chapter *Episcopi* <note>The *Canon Episcopi* was a famous 10th-century legal decree that argued "witchcraft" was a delusion or dream sent by the Devil to trick women</note> reports concerning women deluded by demons—they are nonetheless by no means excused from **heretical depravity** <term>hæretica prauitate: the standard ecclesiastical term for the "wickedness" or "infection" of heresy</term>. For when they are later awake, remembering the renunciation of the Catholic faith and their perverse adoration, **idolatry**, and worship offered to demons, they venerate and pursue all these things. They carefully observe the commands given to them by demons, abstaining from the veneration of the Divine mysteries <note>The Mass and the Eucharist</note> and from sacramental confession regarding the aforementioned things. They also maintain the will and intention of frequenting these gatherings of demons, and they do so out of confidence that through this **pact** <note>original: *confœderationem*</note> with demons, they can perpetrate **harmful magic** <term>maleficia: specific acts of magic intended to cause physical harm, illness, or death</term>, such as carrying out acts of revenge and [bringing about] passions...

<meta>Catchword: fulfilling (original: implen-)</meta>

<summary>Nicolas Jacquier argues that even if the "Sabbath" and encounters with demons are internal delusions or dreams (as suggested by earlier Church law), witches are still guilty of heresy because they consciously embrace and act upon those delusions when they wake up.</summary>

--- Page 223 ---
<meta>This page concludes the argument from page 182 of Nicolas Jacquier’s treatise. Jacquier is finalizing his legal point: that the "dream" defense found in the medieval Canon Episcopi is invalid if the person consciously chooses to follow the demonic path once they wake up.</meta>

<page-num>183</page-num>
<header>Friar Nicolas Jacquier</header>

...to be fulfilled. For it matters nothing to the practice of **heretical depravity** <term>hæretica prauitas: a legal and theological term for the "wickedness" of heresy</term> where it originated, provided that it was accepted with consent and free will. 

Just as if a Christian, while sleeping, were to dream that he heard someone teaching or preaching that it is not possible or true that the consecrated host really contains the true **body of Christ** <note>original: *corpus Christi*</note>; and if, upon waking, he were then to give his consent to that heresy and no longer believe that the body of Christ was in the consecrated host, he would not be excused from heretical depravity, but would be judged as, and would truly be, a Heretic. 

So indeed, even if the **witch-heretics** <note>original: *fascinarij*</note> while sleeping should think they had denied the faith they had received and had worshiped Demons; nonetheless, if afterwards when they are awake these things please them, and they accept and pursue them, they are not excused from heretical depravity, just as that chapter *Episcopi* <note>The *Canon Episcopi* was a 10th-century decree often used to argue that witches were merely dreaming; Jacquier argues here that even if they are dreaming, their waking consent makes them guilty</note> does not excuse those deluded women.

...that these things are always the false dreams of a sick mind, when **Sorcerers** <note>original: "Sortiarij"</note> say they poison the air; nay, rather, it is often and most truly done by them. This can be demonstrated by this very reasoning:

First, because no thought belonging to another, nor any mental fantasy, can be physically felt by us; nor can it, as they say, harm our body in actual reality <note>The author uses "actu ipso" to distinguish between a potential thought and a physical action.</note>. Imagine that I have been killed by you, and picture that in your mind as much as you can—will my good health be diminished or changed even the slightest bit because of it? Not at all. For a person’s vain and false imagination does not transmit contagion, nor does it spread diseases into the bodies of others. Secondly, even in the midst of the **rack** <note>original: "eculeis," a wooden torture frame shaped like a horse.</note> and other torments, they constantly confess that these things were done by them, and they do so most especially when they are led to their execution <note>original: "supplicium."</note> for those crimes.

Finally, the very consensus that appears among all of them confirms our opinion. For in the vain thoughts of the mind, there cannot be one and the same voice from everyone; rather, one person imagines something quite differently from another. For each mind’s action is its own, and there would not be such a conformity of vain thought among so many people dispersed in such various places...

...and agreement, nor could the confession regarding the place itself, the time, and the manner of acting ever be so unified and harmonious among various people, unless these things actually happened in reality, and were exactly as they are said to be done by them. **ANTHONY:** What are you saying, Theophilus?

**THEOPHILUS:** It is clearly so, Anthony. For if they are able to damage the health of men with their **poisons** <note>original: "venenis." In this period, "poison" and "magic potion" were often described by the same word.</note>, diminish the strength and vigor of the body, weaken the nerves, dull the senses, and even disturb the internal **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which pre-modern medicine believed governed health and personality.</note> themselves, why is it surprising if they also hinder that **procreative power** <note>original: "vim illam genitabilem"</note> found in certain reproductive vessels of the human body? This is achieved either by an excessive "cooling" of those very vessels introduced through poison, or by stirring up a certain hatred and loathing in one spouse toward the other (among those they are thus tormenting). I would easily grant that such things are done by them through **satanic art**, yet it is still done so that they may sow discord and strife among those who should enjoy the greatest peace. For in this way, those wicked people take their revenge; they hate those whom they afflict, even though their victims are often undeserving and innocent, acting in imitation of their master, Satan...

...[you might] think or feel. For his way of life was changed, along with his mind and his disposition which loves human society. God can indeed take away or change the very natures and essences of things, but Satan cannot. Therefore, those things which are told about certain **lycanthropes** <term>Lycanthropis: "wolf-men" or werewolves; the belief that humans can physically transform into wolves</term> must also be considered utterly false. 

Although, however, others affirm that this happens among the Northern peoples, such as near the Borysthenes River <note>original: "Borystenem"; the Dnieper River in modern Ukraine</note> and the Tanais <note>original: "Tanaim"; the Don River in Russia</note>. For as to what **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a prolific Roman scholar</note> wrote—that there is a lake in **Arcadia** <note>A region in the Greek Peloponnese famous in mythology for the legend of King Lycaon, who was turned into a wolf</note> which, if people cross it, they turn into wolves—I think it should be understood in this way: that because of the fear which men conceive in crossing that most dangerous lake, they seem to themselves to be wolves. Otherwise, I would call that whole story mere trifles and old wives' tales.

**ANTHONY:** So far you have abundantly explained the kinds of things in which **sorcerers** can rage; now just add one thing: Why can these same impure men also poison and harm with their venoms even pious and truly Christian people? This is something that the most certain and daily experience demonstrates to be true.

**THEOPHILUS:** The solution to this question of yours is easy, Anthony. First, it happens because God, who is most just, punishes the sins of His children for that reason. For those whom we call pious and truly Christian are not without their own failings—not only are they often subject to weaknesses and blemishes, but even to the most serious crimes and sins, as John teaches in 1 John 1, verses 9 and 10: *If we say that we have no sin, we make God a liar.* <note>Theophilus is citing the First Epistle of John to argue that no one is perfectly innocent, and therefore any suffering sent by God is technically "just."</note> Therefore, they are justly afflicted by God. 

Furthermore, through this kind of cross <note>original: "hoc crucis genere"; a common Reformation-era metaphor for any trial or suffering endured by a believer</note>, God tests the patience of His own. For just as He tested His servant Job through the injuries inflicted by those most impious Chaldeans, so He often tries His own people through the poisons and evil deeds <note>original: "maleficia"; a technical legal and theological term for harmful magic intended to cause physical injury or death</note> of **sorcerers** <term>Sortiariorum: those who practice harmful magic, often understood to be in league with the devil</term>, and this for the benefit and salvation of the faithful themselves. For, as Paul says in Romans 5, verse 3: *Affliction produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope, which does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit.* Therefore, the pious ought to bear these very afflictions patiently, so that they may submit themselves to God and conform themselves entirely to His will.

...[no] **sorcerer** <term>Sortiarius: a practitioner of harmful magic, often associated with casting lots or "sortilege"</term> has not entered into a pact and commerce with Satan, and devoted himself to him. So that judges of capital crimes and such wicked deeds may easily recognize this, they take primary care—once these people have been captured—that they be shaven over their whole body and scraped with a razor, lest by chance this **mark** <term>stigma: a physical "Devil's mark," believed to be insensitive to pain, used as evidence in witchcraft trials</term> be hidden under body hair. Therefore, they have contracted a pact <note>original: "Pactum"; referring to the "diabolical pact" central to early modern demonology</note> with Satan, and in turn, having made a formal agreement, they have consented. Satan, indeed, requires that they acknowledge and worship him as God from then on; while they, in turn, require that Satan help them and be present when invoked. And so, out of this pact, Satan succors them and acts according to their prayers and vows; they, in turn, obey his warnings and comply with his will.

**ANTHONY.** But since Satan is by his very nature the most deceitful, or rather the father of lies itself, does he—I ask you—stand by his promises so that he actually fulfills them, as you have described here?

**THEOPHILUS.** Satan is not always a liar, even if he is always a **deceiver** <term>fallax: one who uses trickery or a deceptive appearance to mislead others</term>. For he often speaks the truth in order to entrap those who listen to him. He also frequently fulfills his promises so that we do not take him for a fraud, but rather for a speaker of truth. When Satan spoke concerning Christ our mediator in Mark 1, verse 24: <note>original: "Tu es ille sanctus Dei"</note> "*You are the Holy One of God,*" he was speaking the truth and was not lying. Yet what was his intention then? It was surely so that those who heard these things would later be misled. When he declared the same regarding Paul and Silas in Acts 16, verse 17, with these words: <note>original: "Isti homines serui sunt Dei illius summi, qui annunciant vobis viam salutis"</note> "*These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation,*" he was indeed speaking the truth; yet he was a **fraud** <term>impostor: in this context, someone who uses a true statement to gain a "foot in the door" for later malice</term>, and by that means, he was seeking an entrance for himself to deceive mankind. Thus, when Satan fulfills his promises and keeps the faith he has pledged to **sorcerers** <term>Sortiarij: individuals who have entered a formal agreement with the devil to perform magic</term>, he does this for no other reason than to seduce them more easily and safely afterward, and to better and more tightly win them over and bind them to himself.

**ANTHONY.** Do go on, then, and explain the method by which they operate.

**THEOPHILUS.** This is generally the first method of entering into a **contract** <term>contractus: the "Diabolical Pact," a central theme in 16th-century demonology where a human barters their soul for power</term> between them. In the first place, Satan demands this from them: that they plainly, freely, and openly

# Lambert Daneau

Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) in his work *De Trinitate* (On the Trinity).</note> distinguishes these in Book 3. A **Wonder** <note>original Latin: *Mirum*</note>, therefore, is an extraordinary work, neither common nor ordinary, but one which is nonetheless achieved and produced through natural causes; although these causes are often entirely unknown to us, or known only to a few, or even performed in such a way and by such a method that we humans are neither accustomed to using—even in the same or a similar situation—nor have we even learned how to use.

For example, when that great and ingenious craftsman, and also the supreme philosopher, Archytas of Tarentum <note>A Greek mathematician and statesman (c. 428–347 BC) famous for his mechanical inventions.</note>, displayed a wooden dove flying through the air, that was indeed a wondrous thing, but not a miracle. For that movement was produced in the wooden body by specific counter-weights, and by a certain logic and craftsmanship of lines, and by a construction so precise that one part drew the other along. Therefore, this entire thing was a natural work.

When the same Archytas achieved what Plutarch <note>Greek biographer (c. 46–119 AD) who wrote the *Parallel Lives*.</note> writes in his *Life of Marcellus*—how, while Syracuse <note>A city in Sicily besieged by the Romans under Marcellus in 214–212 BC. For it was done through natural causes and <term>screws <note>original Latin: *cochleas* - likely referring to Archimedean screws or complex pulley systems.</note></term>, according to the rules of mathematicians. In the same way, learned physicians perform many wonders, as do those today called "mechanics," yet these are not miracles. # Dialogue on Sorcerers

...is it permitted for us to use the help and labor of **sorcerers** <term>sortiarii: specifically those who use "sortes" or lots for divination and magic</term>, so that we might apply some remedy to our ills?

**THE.** Some people make a distinction in this matter. For they think that if a **magistrate** <term>magistratus: a civil authority or government official</term> wishes and commands us to do so, we can then use their help and remedies with a safe conscience. Otherwise, however, they contend it is neither permitted nor even divinely lawful <note>original: "fas," referring to law as ordained by God</note>. Therefore, they say that when the magistrate himself orders them to bring us aid, but we do not implore their help ourselves, we do not commit a **sin** <term>peccatum: a transgression against divine law</term> if we admit them. But if we ourselves turn to them of our own accord, then they say we implore their help, we flatter and applaud them, and we invite them to us in a friendly manner. In this, a grave sin is committed. But if the magistrate himself wills and commands it to be done without our asking, then we experience their help almost against our will; in this case, we are free from any moral hesitation or guilt. For the authority of the magistrate intervenes as if it were the authority of God himself, whom it is necessary to obey, because he holds his power from God. This, therefore, is the foundation or support of that distinction.

But see, Antonius, how weak that foundation is—indeed, how vain and false. First, Paul generally forbids in Romans 3, verse 8, that we should ever do evil so that good may come from it, by whatever authority one might be ordered to do—

<summary>Theophilus examines the argument that using sorcery is acceptable if ordered by a civil magistrate, ultimately dismissing this distinction as a false justification for doing evil.</summary>

-> Lambert Daneau <-

...be commanded, whether by a judge and magistrate, or by anyone else. Next, I believe we may argue by analogy <note>original: "à pari," a logical argument from similar cases</note>. If a judge and magistrate should command us to worship idols, to steal, to commit adultery, or to embrace Satan, can we then do those things with a safe **conscience** <term>conscientia: the internal sense of right and wrong guided by God</term>, just because the magistrate commands it? No one of sound mind, I am certain, would ever grant that.

Furthermore, when that same magistrate commands that a **sorcerer** <term>sortiarius: specifically a practitioner of magic or divination</term> help us with his satanic works, and openly instructs us to present ourselves to be cured in that manner and commit ourselves to him, and we do so: then we are perpetrating and consenting to evil.

Therefore, even if we had to lie sick in bed for the entire course of our lives, we must not resort to this kind of help and the arts of **Satan**, even if the magistrate—even the highest magistrate—wills and commands it. For that cannot be done without our acknowledging the powers of Satan, whose help we would be using and in whom we would be acquiescing; yet, through our **baptism**, we have completely and long ago renounced him. Nor, truly, is it in the power of Satan to bring it about that we either live or die, but in the power of God alone.

This much can indeed be considered and granted: that if someone who is said to be a sorcerer is able—not through any superstitious means nor any commerce with Satan, but according to the rules and precepts of **physicians** <term>medicorum: those practicing legitimate medicine</term> and through permitted medicines...

(Deo Optimo Maximo), a title meaning "To God, the Best and Greatest," originally used for Jupiter but adopted by Renaissance Christians for the Father</note>, our parent, in prayers, whether we are rising from our bed in the morning or when we go to lie down for sleep.

For if we commit ourselves to the protection of God—who is the highest king, the most discerning father, and who bridles and restrains Satan himself and his powers—He surrounds us with a host of angels for our guard. If, I say, He is for us, who shall harm us? 

Scripture itself testifies to this: *If God is for us, who can be against us?* <note>Romans 8:31; the original text cites verse 30, but this famous phrase appears in verse 31</note>. Therefore, above all, we must diligently meditate upon that most sweet and excellent promise of God, which was made to us through our Lord Jesus Christ and stands in very eloquent words in Psalm 91, expressed thus by Buchanan <note>George Buchanan (1506–1582), a Scottish scholar whose Latin poetic paraphrases of the Psalms were famous throughout Europe</note>:

> ->*If you believe your safety, wealth, children, and home*<-
> ->*Are to be protected by the counsel of God,*<-
> ->*When insane fortune shall thunder,*<-
> ->*If you flee under the shadow of the Lord,*<-

For he established that all things are indeed filled with likenesses or images (which he himself called *eidola* <note>original: εἴδωλα. In Epicurean philosophy, these are thin films of atoms shed by objects; Epicurus used them to explain both vision and the "ghosts" seen in dreams or hallucinations.</note>), but that these are empty and hollow. And when once, for the sake of frightening him, certain young men dressed as Furies made a loud noise and a ruckus around the tomb they knew he had entered, he is said to have remained calmly unmoved, merely ordering them to desist from such follies.

I am not sure whether Aristotle would have ever granted that there is some nature of the soul or spirit that could move about without its own proper body, or wrap itself in some body of its own fashioning at its own whim. ## On the Obsolescence of Oracles

[...of that] divine [spirit] <note>Completes the word *divini* from the previous page.</note> whom Plato celebrates, one who is most foreign to it has thus invented and fashioned things most abhorrent to the common sense of men. However, that entire reasoning is derived from this source: that there are certain intermediate natures placed between the divine and the human, which they have called by the name of Demons <note>original: *Dæmonum*. In the Platonic tradition, a *daimon* is a "spirit" or "power" that acts as a bridge between the realm of the gods and the realm of mortals.</note>. The author of the *Epinomis* <note>An ancient Greek dialogue attributed to Plato, or his student Philip of Opus, serving as an "appendix" to the *Laws*.</note>, that is, the appendix to Plato’s books on *The Laws* (for it is well known that there has been doubt about this authorship), having placed them in the third and middle region, clearly makes them an aerial race. And he attributes to them the affection of both joy and sadness, of which he says the divine race is free, and he makes them interpreters for men before the Gods; but later writers have produced this race even from fire and water.

There exist also the writings of Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (11th century), a Byzantine scholar whose work *On the Operation of Demons* classified various types of spirits.</note> concerning these spirits, which antiquity clearly made into living creatures, that is *zoa* <note>original: ζῶα</note>; though what sort of writings they are, let the readers judge. Nor do those things differ much from these which are read throughout the writings of Philo the Jew <note>Philo of Alexandria, a 1st-century Jewish philosopher who used Platonic concepts to explain Hebrew scripture.</note> concerning these Natures that participate in both a certain divinity and humanity: indeed, he is more of a "Platonizer" <note>original: *Platonissantis*. This refers to the famous ancient saying, "Either Plato Philo-nizes or Philo Plato-nizes," because their styles were so similar.</note> in opinion and sentiment than in speech and style. And these disputations altogether attribute bodies to those spirits. But since the nature of the soul for Plato is also without a body, the nature of these spirits will surely be one thing, and the nature of souls in themselves another. In the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul.</note> indeed, [he mentions] that certain phantom-images <note>original: *simulachra*</note> are seen, and not those of just any [souls]...

Concerning images, or likenesses, or visions and specters—how wonderfully those who wished to explain Platonic writings in their commentaries have disagreed! These authors teach, among other things, that those likenesses or visions are certain substantial things which demons fabricate through a particular art. For as <term>Proclus</term> <note>Proclus (412–485 CE) was one of the last major Greek philosophers and a key figure in Neoplatonism.</note> says: *According to Plato, appearances are the substantial realities of certain images created by a demonic mechanism.* <note>original Greek: κατὰ πλάτωνα αἱ ἐμφάσεις ὑποστάσεις εἰσὶν εἰδώλων τινῶν δαιμονίᾳ μηχανῇ δημιουργύμεναι.</note>

Such things indeed seem to be stated quite boldly in philosophical disputes. In this way, no room would be left for the investigation of any causes, since for everything there would be a ready-made "divine efficiency" at hand. The student who was mocked in the schools did not give such a bad answer when, upon being asked: "In what way does snow exist?" he replied: "Because God willed it so." <note>The author is poking fun at philosophers who use "spirits" or "God" as a shortcut to avoid explaining natural science.</note>

In philosophical disputes, however, to aid the grasp of the human mind, diverse things have been well and usefully distinguished by specific names: those that are substantial and true are called <term>substances</term> <note>original Greek: ὑποστάσεις (*hypostases*). In philosophy, this refers to the underlying reality or essence of a thing.</note>; those that are apparent and empty are called <term>appearances</term> <note>original Greek: ἐμφάσεις (*emphases*). Here used to describe reflections or optical illusions rather than physical matter.</note>. For example, a man’s face is a **substance** <note>original Greek: ὑπόστασίς.</note>, but in a mirror...
