...of this, an image, or **appearances** <note>original Greek: *ἐμφάσεις* (*emphaseis*). In this context, it refers to reflections or the visual manifestation of a spirit or idea.</note>. To confuse these things for the unlearned, and to create substantial and "true" things out of dreams and visions, seems quite ridiculous. And I do not know if that foreign opinion is truly entangled in the original **Platonic decrees**.

How variously and in what a discordant manner do they recount these things, just so that each might carve out exactly what they want! For they attempt to explain those matters:

*   **Logically** <note>original Greek: *λογικῶς* (*logikōs*)</note>, that is, only by means of argumentation;
*   And to illustrate them **practically** <note>original Greek: *πραγματικῶς* (*pragmatikōs*)</note> with examples;
*   And to indicate them **theologically** <note>original Greek: *θεολογικῶς* (*theologikōs*)</note>, which are the applications of poetic fables;
*   And to demonstrate them **physically** <note>original Greek: *φυσικῶς* (*physikōs*)</note>, that is, by providing natural causes;

...and finally, to heap all of these things together with **Egyptian fictions** <note>original: *Aegyptiacis cōmentis*. This likely refers to the "Hermetic" or mystical traditions that Renaissance scholars often associated with ancient Egypt.</note>.

I am truly ashamed—though I am by no means an opponent of **Platonic Philosophy**—of such explanations. That "family" <note>The author refers to the Neoplatonists as a "family" or school of thought.</note> delighted in mixing and involving everything in these explanations, creating as it were illusions and pretenses. They did not clarify the meaning of the author [Plato] whom they professed to follow, but rather obscured it.

Indeed, I wonder if those very interpreters ever possessed anything certain or well-explored upon which their thoughts might rest as on a firm foundation. And yet, certain **Ecclesiastical writers** <note>The "Church Fathers" or early Christian theologians.</note>, embracing these trifles, have forced them into the sound doctrine of heavenly truth like the **dreams of sick men** <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for incoherent or irrational ideas.</note>. A work of multifaceted study and singular industry, which I am not sure should ever be neglected by those devoted to wisdom. **Cicero** wrote excellently: <note>original: "Ut Deos esse natura opinamur, sic permanere animos arbitramur." From Cicero's *Tusculan Disputations* (1.36).</note> "Just as we believe by nature that the Gods exist, so we judge that souls endure." He [Cicero] considers the rest to be fabrications <note>referring to the more gruesome descriptions of the underworld</note> designed for the terror of children and the unlearned. 

The **Homeric** souls, indeed, are similar to shadows or the visions of dreams; such is that image of **Hercules** in the underworld, while he himself enjoyed marriage with **Youth** <note>original: *Iuuentutis*; referring to the goddess Hebe, personification of youth</note> in heaven. As these are the inventions of myths, so it must be believed that there is some underlying reason why those stories were devised. 

For if anyone were to deny that certain appearances <note>original: *species*; ghosts, phantoms, or spiritual manifestations</note> present themselves not only to those sleeping but also to those awake, he would seem too bold, or rather, too rash. Consider what was presented as an error to **Pentheus** <note>In Greek mythology, King Pentheus of Thebes was driven mad for refusing to acknowledge the divinity of Dionysus</note>, whom the Tragedies claim was incited to monstrous crimes by those **Maenads** <note>The female followers of Dionysus (Bacchus), known for their wild, ecstatic rituals</note>: must this not be attributed to some external malignant power? 

Regarding the furies of **Orestes** and similar torments <note>Orestes was famously hounded by the Furies (Eumenides) after avenging his father by killing his mother, Clytemnestra</note>, although **Marcus Cicero** refers these to the terrors and tortures of the mind <note>i.e., a psychological interpretation of guilt rather than literal demons</note>, it should not therefore be asserted that nothing of that kind truly exists and occurs in reality. # On the Obsolescence of Oracles <note>original: "De defectu oraculorum"; the title of a famous dialogue by Plutarch exploring why the ancient Greek oracles had ceased to speak</note>

... **Lucretius** <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BCE), the Roman poet whose work "On the Nature of Things" is the primary source for Epicurean physics</note> preferred to give incorrect causes for things rather than to violate the **trust of the senses**, which he believed to be the foundation of life and safety. But it is not my current purpose to inquire into anyone's doctrine with such precision. Let us, therefore, follow the **Epicurean** arguments. While these arguments attribute the entire power of judgment to the senses, they nonetheless say this: "The sense," they claim, "is a fragile thing, fluid and capable of error."

The **thought of the mind** itself, however, is even much sharper and swifter; it is accustomed to stir the senses and turn them toward any empty appearance or a thing that has no substance at all. For just as a true figure is easily expressed, so when the human mind grasps both that which it fashions and the process of fashioning itself, it is perfectly ready to shape whatever it pleases by varying the details. 

This can be observed in the manifold shifting of **dreams** in those who sleep, occurring in that faculty where visions are represented—which the Greeks called the *phantastikon* <note>original: "φαντασικὸν"; the imaginative faculty or the power of representation in the mind</note>—where, starting from a slight impulse, it turns itself about, giving rise to various states and **images** <note>original: "simulachris"</note> of dreams. Indeed, the nature of that faculty is to be in continual motion, and that very motion constitutes certain visions and thoughts. It would be a long task to review the Epicurean theories regarding these **images** or **likenesses** <term>simulachra</term> <note>In Epicurean physics, these are thin films of atoms that constantly peel off the surface of objects and fly through the air; when they strike our eyes or minds, they create the sensation of seeing the object</note>, which they claim are emitted from all things and before our eyes...

### On the Little Book of Plutarch,
<note>original: "In libellum Plutarchi"; this refers to Plutarch’s essay "On the Obsolescence of Oracles"</note>

Should all antiquity be thought to have lied about **Spirits of the Dead** and **Ghosts**? <note>original: "Lemuribus & laruis"; Lemures were the restless spirits of the dead in Roman religion, while larvae were malevolent, haunting ghosts</note> Should all the monstrous visions—among which that of **Marcus Brutus** is the most celebrated—be dismissed as mere trifles? <note>According to Plutarch, a giant, terrifying specter appeared to the Roman general Brutus before the Battle of Philippi, identifying itself as his "evil spirit"</note> Nor should anyone claim that none of these things were truly said simply because he himself has not seen them. For who, being even slightly prudent, would seem likely to tolerate such a view? Indeed, just as one must decide through defense what has been truly or falsely handed down in the **Histories**, so to judge by mere opinion what was done or not done in this supernatural category would be far too arrogant, and not far removed from madness.

By this same audacity, it is denied that certain people—through an external force working its way into them—can either prophesy while in a frenzy or perform other wonderful deeds. What then? Was it not necessary for the entire power and effectiveness of the ancient oracles to be contained in and driven by some such agitation from an external nature? Regarding these matters, there exist mentions of many others, as well as the wordy and terrifying narrative of **Lucan** in his fifth book. <note>The poet Lucan, in his epic *Pharsalia*, gives a famously gruesome description of the Delphic priestess being violently possessed by the god Apollo while delivering an oracle</note>

Do we not think that **Panic terrors** <note>Sudden, groundless fears attributed to the god Pan</note> were excited by a similar madness? 

Then there is the matter of enchantments and spells—that is, **incantations** <note>original: "ἐπωδῶν" (epōdōn)</note>—and those things which they called **amulets**. An example of this was the tiny golden image belonging to **Sulla**, which he received from the **Delphic Apollo**... <note>The Roman dictator Sulla was said to have carried a small golden figure of Apollo taken from the temple at Delphi, which he would pray to in times of danger</note>

# On the Cessation of Oracles.
<note>original: *De defectu oraculorum*. This is the title of a famous work by Plutarch, but here serves as a heading for the author's Christian commentary on why ancient pagan oracles fell silent.</note>

I shall speak of the influence of spirits, by which we have heard that some people were gladdened and helped in difficult circumstances, while others were afflicted and worn down by spirits that had been provoked and offended. Indeed, these matters were of such a kind that those spirits reigned throughout the world as if by a granted right, keeping the minds and bodies of men oppressed. In this state, neither judgment, nor intelligence, nor reason, nor will possessed their proper freedom and integrity; instead, the senses and emotions of the body were forced to serve a foreign will. 

But when the Son of God was born on earth, he joined human nature to his own divine nature in such a way that both were united in the one man, Jesus. He had been destined from the beginning and promised by divine oracles—a king of all nations born on earth from the **Davidic line** <note>The lineage of King David, from which the Messiah was prophesied to emerge.</note>, known by the Hebrew name **Messiah**, which the Greeks translated as **Christ**. <note>original: *Messiæ... It was these spirits who ultimately provided the cause for his death, by which he was removed from our midst through the greatest possible insult. Yet, by that very death, the strength and power of those spirits were destroyed. Although he died and was buried, he was soon raised and brought back to life by divine power. These usually inflict even heavier blows when that force occupies, as it were, the **fortress** of human nature and reduces the mind to its own power and dominion—the mind, which is the fountain of reason and counsel, from which all actions in human life flow. For how miserable and deplorable it is for this to happen...

...what is brought from Tragedy? As when the wrath of Demons harms and presses upon someone:
> *First of all, let the health of a sound mind be taken from the soul, and let it be turned into this perverse judgment, so that he does not even understand that he himself is sinning.* <note>original: "Primum omnium ex animo auferatur sanitas..." This is a Latin translation of a Greek tragic fragment (often attributed to the poet Lycurgus or Euripides) illustrating the concept of *Até*: the divine madness that leads a person to their own destruction.</note>

For this is a deadly perversity: either to rush into sins with contempt and stubbornness, or to apply a cunning defense of malice to support these actions as if to prop them up. Therefore, the ancient custom of religious piety held that the power of Demons was effective not only in those (whom they called by the Greek word <term>energoumenoi</term> <note>original: ἐνεργουμένους; literally "those worked upon" or "the energized." But regarding these matters, if anyone wished to explain them fully, a whole new and different discourse would have to be started. We have already strayed beyond our intended purpose and have been more wordy than we ought to have been at this time.

## THE DEFINITION OF SUPERSTITION, explained.

For superstition—as it is held by the Doctors <term>original: Doctoribus; the authoritative theologians and Fathers of the Church</term> and regarding that passage in Colossians 2 <note>Colossians 2:23: "Which things have indeed a show of wisdom in superstition and humility..." (Douay-Rheims translation).</note>—those things "which have an appearance of wisdom in superstition," is Religion observed beyond measure. It possesses the appearance of wisdom not in truth, but in falsehood; it is abundant where there is no usefulness, but exists through human wisdom which, as is said in James 3 <note>James 3:15.</note>, is "earthly, sensual, and devilish." Likewise, Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a central figure in medieval theology.</note> says in the gloss <term>A "gloss" is a standard commentary written in the margins or between the lines of the Bible.</term> on that same passage: "Superstition is a feigned Religion, so that things which are false may seem true; it humbles minds toward earthly things, so that they are not raised up to heavenly things." And Nicholas <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan whose biblical commentaries were the most widely used in the late Middle Ages.</note> in the same place defines superstition as "superfluous and vain Religion." From these, it follows that superstition is Religion observed beyond measure—that is, with evil and defective methods and circumstances.

For a fuller explanation of this, however, it should be noted what Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note> says in the *Secunda Secundae* <term>original: secunda secundæ; the second part of the second part of the *Summa Theologiae*, Aquinas’s comprehensive guide to theology and ethics.</term>, Question 92, Article 1. Superstition, he says, is a vice opposed to religion by way of excess, offering more in divine worship than true Religion does; because it offers divine worship <term>original: cultum diuinum; the outward acts of devotion or ritual</term> either to someone it should not, or in a manner that it should not, insofar as something is done in divine worship that ought not to be done.

<summary>Martin de Arles provides the formal theological definition of superstition as "religion observed beyond measure" or "excessive religion," drawing on the Bible, Gregory the Great, and Thomas Aquinas.</summary>
<keywords>superstition, religion, excess, Thomas Aquinas, Gregory the Great, Nicholas of Lyra, divine worship, false wisdom</keywords>

[...ought to] be. But the act of submerging the image (which these people do) is of this kind. And if their whole act is rendered evil because of one bad circumstance—since according to Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-century mystical theologian. <sig>Z 3</sig>

[absolute] quantity, and according to this measure there cannot be anything superfluous in **divine worship**, because man can do nothing that is not less than what he owes to God. In another way, a thing can be superfluous according to the <term>quantity of proportion</term> <note>original: "quantitatem proportionis"; a technical term in Scholastic philosophy meaning that the means used are not properly fitted to the goal being sought.</note>, specifically because it is not proportional to its purpose. For the purpose of **divine worship** is that man gives glory to God and subjects himself to Him in mind and body.

And therefore, whatever a man does that pertains to the glory of God, and to this end—that the mind of man is subjected to God, and also the body through the moderate restraint of desires—according to the ordinance of God and the Church, and the custom of those with whom a man lives before God, is not superfluous in **divine worship**.

If, however, there is something that, by its very nature, does not pertain to God's glory, nor to the fact that the mind of man is carried toward God, or that the inordinate desires of the flesh are restrained—or even if it is outside the institution of God and the Church, or against common custom (which according to **Augustine** must be held as law) <note>St. Augustine famously argued that the long-standing customs of the Christian community should be respected as having the force of law.</note>—all of this is to be considered superfluous and **superstitious**. This is because, consisting only in outward things, it does not pertain to the interior worship of God. Hence **Augustine**, in his book *On True Religion*, introduces what is said in **Luke 17**. <note>The text likely refers to Luke 17:21: "The kingdom of God is within you," supporting the author's point that true worship is internal.</note>

### That the IMMERSION of images, no matter how much it is performed with hymns and songs, amounts to an injury to the saints and is a superstitious act.

It is clear, however, that to submerge an image of the **blessed Peter** does not pertain to the glory of God—by which the Lord is praised in His saints—but rather to reproach and injury. Nor is it according to the ordinance of God and the Church, which has ordained that the images of the saints are to be venerated <note>original: "adorentur." In this context, the author refers to the theological concept of *dulia*, or the honor shown to saints through their images, rather than the worship (*latria*) reserved for God alone.</note>, as will be discussed below. On the contrary, no nation or country has commonly ever attempted to do such things; therefore, it must be concluded that this act is entirely evil and superstitious. If there were any divine power <note>original: "numinis"; referring to a spiritual or supernatural presence or efficacy.</note> present in such an observance, theologians and religious and devoted men would surely be the ones to better understand and safeguard that observance. Yet the opposite is found to be true, because they discourage it, reprove it, and prohibit it; therefore, such a rite passes into superstition, which is nothing other than *vain religion*, as was [said] above.

# *HE INTRODUCES CERTAIN PRO- positions concerning specific superstitious acts performed on the feast day of Saint John the Baptist, and the blessed Peter and Paul.*

**The second proposition:** although on the feast day of the Nativity of **Saint John the Baptist** <note>Celebrated on June 24th, coinciding with the summer solstice and traditional midsummer folk customs.</note> many things are piously performed by the faithful for the sake of celebration—for instance, the ringing of bells and "fires of joy" <note>original: "ignes iocunditatis," referring to the traditional Midsummer or St. John's Eve bonfires.</note>—and similarly, at early dawn they go out to collect fragrant, excellent, and medicinal herbs which are at their peak of natural power and virtue because of the season; yet there are certain common people so superstitious that they believe these things, which are done for the solemnity and joy of the feast, are actually performed as superstitious remedies. 

For instance, they believe the ringing of bells is for driving away spirits or evildoers. Some light fires at the crossroads of the fields so that **sorceresses** <term>sortilegæ</term> <note>Literally "lot-casters," those who predict the future or perform magic using lots.</note> and **witches** <term>maleficæ</term> <note>Literally "evil-doers," specifically those believed to use magic to cause physical harm.</note> do not pass through there on that night—as I myself have seen with my own eyes. Others, burning the herbs collected on Saint John’s day to protect against lightning, thunder, and storms, believe that by their smoke they can keep away demons and tempests. This is common among our people, and I have taken care to reprimand it many times during my episcopal visitation. Others do this or that on that day supersti-

->tiously<-

Nor, however, should we deny that those herbs possess medicinal power for creating fumigations <note>The practice of burning herbs to produce therapeutic smoke.</note> against the illnesses of children and even of **beasts of burden** <term>iumentorum</term>. Furthermore, in the collection of any medicinal herbs at any time, it is not permitted to employ any observations or incantations, except for the **Divine Symbol** <note>The Apostles' Creed.</note> or the **Lord’s Prayer** <note>The "Our Father."</note>, so that only the Creator and God of all might be honored, as Saint **Thomas Aquinas** says in the *Secunda Secundæ*, question 96, article 4.

Nor do I see why these blacksmiths or metalworkers <note>original: "fabri ferrarij siue mulciberi." Mulciber was an epithet for the Roman god Vulcan, here used for smiths.</note> choose the day of Saint John the Baptist and the day of the Apostles Peter and Paul to precisely bleed or **phlebotomize** <term>fleubothonizent</term> <note>The medical practice of opening a vein to let blood, used historically for both humans and animals.</note> horses and other livestock rather than other days during the same season; instead, this seems superstitious and suggested by the devil, so that the days and festivities of such great saints are desecrated <note>original: "soluantur"; literally "loosened" or "dissolved," implying a breaking of the religious reverence due to the day.</note> against divine reverence. ### THAT THE RINGING OF SIGNALS or bells on the night of Saint Agatha is not done to ward off these sorceresses and witches, as some foolishly believe, but for other reasons.

Consequently, an argument from authority should be made regarding **Theology**. ### *THAT ALL DAYS OF THE YEAR are good, and in every year, and on every day, and at every hour of the day, it is good and praiseworthy to begin any holy, lawful, and honorable works.*

Now, therefore, let us prove through <term>theology</term> <note>The study of religious belief and the nature of God, which in the Middle Ages was considered the "Queen of the Sciences."</note> that the observance of these particular days is vain and superstitious. We shall do this by putting forward several conclusions collected from the Doctors of the Church, especially from Master **Jean Gerson** <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), the influential Chancellor of the University of Paris and a prominent critic of magic and superstition.</note>. The first conclusion is this: All days of the year are the works of the Most High God. This is evident from the text of Holy Scripture in **Genesis 1**, where throughout the entire chapter the works of the six days are described, and how the first works of God were days and years. Furthermore, the Most High God began to work the first good thing from that which is good and best; and the Creator of all things is the highest and the best, therefore all His works are good. As it says in Genesis 1: *God saw all the things that He had made, and they were very good.* Therefore days and years, since they are primary...

> Your is the day, and yours is the night; you have fashioned the dawn and the sun. <note>original: "Tuus est dies, & tua est nox, tu fabricatus es auroram & solem." Psalm 74:16 (Vulgate 73:16).</note>

### THE SECOND CONCLUSION

All days of the year are good, and in every year, and on every day and every hour of the day, it is good and praiseworthy to begin, perform, work at, and profess any works that are holy, lawful, and honorable. Understand this to be the case unless it is forbidden by a precept of God or the Church—just as on certain feast days, specific types of laborious work are prohibited. 

The first part of this conclusion is evident from what was said in the preceding conclusion: because days and years are the works of the highest and infinite goodness. Moreover, it is the nature of the best being to bring forth the best things. Therefore, to say that any day is evil by its own nature is to do an injury to God, who is the craftsman <note>original: "artifex."</note> of days and years; for an evil work implies malice in the craftsman. 

The second part is also evident: just as days, years, and even the hours of the day proceed from God the creator, so too every holy, lawful, and honorable work—which is begun and finished on any day or at any hour—is directed, begun, and finished by the Lord, as the Lord says:
> Without me you can do nothing. <note>original: "Sine me nihil potestis facere." John 15:5.</note>

And again:
> All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. <note>original: "Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil." John 1:3.</note>

From these things it follows that it is a superstitious and vain belief—and one deservedly to be condemned—to refuse to begin, work on, or finish a good or holy work (not otherwise prohibited by the Church) on specific years or days. This position is expressly the mind of the **Apostle** <note>St. Paul the Apostle, whose letters form a major part of the New Testament.</note> against those similar to the people to whom he wrote in **Galatians chapter 4**. This is also found in the text of **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note> in the *Decretum* <note>The Decretum Gratiani, a collection of Canon Law.</note> 25, question 7, *Quis*, where he argues against and rebukes those of Galatia, saying:

> I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain <note>original: "sine casu" (likely a transcription error for the biblical "sine causa").</note> by preaching according to the Catholic faith. 

He rejects all these practices as superstitious and vain. However, this does not apply if such an observation of days is done out of reverence for the holiness of some solemn feast day, or out of devotion to one of the saints. # THE BELIEF THAT IMAGES OF BRONZE, lead, or white or red wax, or other materials—baptized, exorcised, or rather desecrated through Magic arts—and that on certain days they possess marvelous powers which are recounted in the books of such arts, is an error against the faith.

Chapter 14, Lesson 160. It is said that in his own times, a certain person in London was cured of a **quartan fever** <term>a recurring fever, often associated with malaria, where paroxysms occur every fourth day</term> through a golden image of a **Lion** made under a specific constellation. He says that it is difficult to judge whether this is true, given the wonderful operations of the celestial bodies; for he states it is certain that nothing of this kind is illicit if it can be accomplished through the laws of nature. 

However, he responds by citing **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority used in this text.</note> in the book, question, article, and location cited above, where the Holy Doctor <note>A traditional title for Aquinas.</note> cites the blessed **Augustine** in the 10th book of *The City of God*. He argues that the opinion of **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–c. 305 AD) who suggested that physical objects could be imbued with divine or spiritual power.</note> was false regarding the construction of such images. 

It is true, indeed, that natural things receive their forms and virtues from the celestial bodies. However, **artificial images** can acquire no virtue from the "art" of their making, nor can they possess any power other than that which they already have by reason of their material. A shape or figure is not a principle of physical change; therefore, the gold of such an image has no more power to cause an effect than any other gold of a different shape. 

If such an image does produce another effect, this is due to the work of **demons**, who, according to Augustine, are the deceivers of men. Therefore, such images obtain their power "astronomically" only through a demon. The sign of this is that they use, along with those images, certain **characters**... <note>original: "characteres" — specialized magical signs, symbols, or sigils often inscribed on talismans.</note>

# THAT THOSE ENTERING INTO A PACT with demons, whether tacit or express, are Idolaters, Heretics, and estranged from the Catholic faith.

**Third conclusion.** Just as true and **Christian faith** works wonders in those who believe rightly, so too does a **false and evil belief**—by God’s permission—sometimes bring about evil outcomes, or rather, earns them as a punishment. The **Apostle** <note>original: "Apostolus"; referring to Saint Paul</note> develops the first part of this point at length through examples in **Hebrews 11**, but the **Gospels** themselves speak much concerning the power of faith. 

The remaining part of this conclusion is experienced daily among those of **misguided belief** and the **superstitious**, whom **GOD** punishes in this way because of their bad faith. Indeed, when the Lord recognizes that someone adheres too much to certain **vain observances** <note>original: "vanis obseruantijs"; rituals or customs that have no basis in nature or the Church, such as lucky charms or omens</note>, He permits certain outcomes to occur. In this way, they are consequently strengthened even further in their misguided opinion, so that their blindness increases, and they fall into the **snare** which they prepared for themselves. 

Through these things, therefore, sin occurs because men are deceived through the **cooperation of demons** on account of their preceding false belief. For this reason, those who observe such superstitions receive many misfortunes because of their **false faith**—hardships which others, who do not care for such things, do not suffer at all.

## THAT THOSE WHO OBSERVE DAYS
### and years, through their own false imagination, attribute whatever evil happens to the malice of the day and year, acting as diviners.

Furthermore, while the imagination of those who observe days and years is focused too narrowly upon such days, whatever evil occurs, they attribute it to the "malice" of the day by way of divination <note>original: "auguriantes"; referring to the practice of reading omens to predict the future</note>. For example: someone is thrown from an unbridled and wild horse on a slippery road, or is drowned in a river; immediately the common folk, as soon as they hear of it, will assign the causes of this kind of misfortune in various ways—things which are, in fact, in no way the cause of the accident. 

One will say that upon leaving the house he encountered a cat or a hare; or that in stepping out of the door he tripped his foot; or that in the morning he put his shirt on inside-out <note>original: "camisiam auersam"; literally "a turned shirt"</note>, or that the right shoe was put on the left foot. **Caesar Augustus** <note>The first Roman Emperor (63 BC – 14 AD). That is, men initiate the war and God the victory. From
all of which it is concluded, that the
observation of days for the purpose of achieving some

from God working miraculously, nor from

# THAT CERTAIN OLD WOMEN ARE SUPERSTITIOUS
## *who attach small slips of paper, or what are commonly called "names," against fevers, along with certain vain observations.*

In the same way, certain old women are superstitious who attach small sheets of paper—or "names" <note>original: "nomina"; these were amulets or slips of paper inscribed with holy names or pseudo-magical characters believed to have healing powers</note> as they are commonly called—even containing Catholic words. Furthermore, regarding the person for whom this is tied—or to whom they have given some herb to eat to drive away fevers—they say this is of no value unless he receives it toward the sun at its rising, with knees bent. I remember an old woman once saying this to me when I was suffering from fever myself. This, I say, is superstitious and vain, and utterly lacking in reason.

"Write this on virgin parchment; let it be carried in a triangular shape with unknown characters; let it be censed with incense and hung from the neck; and let these things be done at certain hours. Then, within three days—or before three days pass—the effect we seek will undoubtedly follow." Rather, this...

It is in this way that we understand what is written in Genesis 3: "that the serpent was more cunning than all the living things" <note>original: "serpens callidior erat cunctis animantibus"; Genesis 3:1.</note>. This cunning is principally to be referred to the demon who appeared in the serpent; but it is not referred to the serpent itself, except insofar as it was moved by the cunning of the demon—just as a person’s tongue is called "learned" because it is prudently moved by the intellect. 

Whence it follows: "and the Lord said to the serpent" <note>Genesis 3:14.</note>. The gloss <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard collection of medieval biblical commentaries.</note> says: "that is, to the Devil who was hiding and speaking in the serpent." Thus, the curse is placed upon the serpent <note>i.e., the punishment is directed at the vessel used by the Devil.</note>. We can, therefore, adjure demons in irrational creatures through the virtue of the divine name, and repel them as enemies, lest they [harm] <note>The catchword *ceant* indicates the next page begins with *noceant* (harm).</note> us.

...against the lie, especially the most pernicious kind, which occurs in those matters pertaining to the Christian Religion. A lie, moreover, is when someone outwardly signifies the contrary of the truth. It is, then, contrary to the truth to adjure a fable <note>original: "fabellam"; referring back to the description of the creature Sabella</note>; contrary, I say, not only to Physical truth, but also to Theological truth. 

Regarding the Physical, it is obvious. For nothing of such a kind can be found among natural things, which are contained within certain determined genera and species. For according to the Philosopher <note>original: "Philo."; an abbreviation for Aristotle, who was known simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval scholarship</note> in the second book *On the Soul* <note>original: "2. de anima"</note>: 

> For all things consisting of nature, there is a set limit and a proportion <note>original: "ratio"</note> of size and growth, and this comes from the soul. 

Hence, since every single animal has its own proper species, size, and operation: if, therefore, this monster has its head in the clouds and its feet in the sea, reaching from the sea all the way to the clouds, then it shall not be numbered among natural things according to the rule stated above. 

It is also repugnant to Theological truth that such a thing exists, because all created things in the nature of reality were created by God, and insofar as they exist, they are good. Genesis 1: 
> God saw all the things he had made, and they were very good. 

Now, the nature of the "good" consists in mode, species, and order <note>The triad of "modus, species, et ordo" was a standard Scholastic definition of being, drawn from St. Augustine</note>, which pertain to the essence of any species, as Saint Thomas says in the First Part [of the *Summa Theologiae*], Question 8, Article 5 <note>The author likely intended Question 5, Article 5, where Aquinas discusses "mode, species, and order" as the constituents of goodness</note>, through

<note>Treatise on Superstitions</note>

By **mode**, moreover, is meant the determination, or the proportioning <note>original: "commensuratio"</note> of the principles, whether of the materials or of the efficient causes <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note> that produce the thing itself. The **form** itself is signified by **species**, because it is through form that each thing is established within a specific kind. From the form, moreover, follows an inclination toward a purpose <note>original: "finem"; literally "end" or "goal"</note>, or toward an action, or toward something of this sort, and this pertains to **order**. 

Hence, the nature of the "good," insofar as it consists in perfection, consists also in mode, species, and order. That is to say: for a thing to be perfect and good, and created by God—and if it is a natural or corporeal thing—it is required that it possess essential principles. It must, I mean, have a determined matter in relation to a determined form, which gives being to the thing, and through which it is placed in a specific category <note>original: "specie"</note>, and consequently possesses its own proper operation. 

But none of these things exist in this "fable of a monster" <note>original: "monstro fabella"</note>; therefore, there is no good in it, and consequently, it is not from God. This is clear because, in the same question—as the Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> cites Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> in the book *On the Nature of Good*—these three things (**mode**, **species**, and **order**) are present as general goods in things made by God. Where these three are great, there are great goods; where they are small, there are small goods. Where they are non-existent, there is no good at all. Therefore, such a monster does not exist among natural things by God's hand, nor will it ever be 

<meta>catchword: Deus (God)</meta>

# THAT THE ACT OF SUBMERSION of images and relics is a sacrilege, and what sacrilege is.

Now it follows how that act—namely, of submerging the image of Saint Peter—is a sacrilege <note>The author is likely referring to a superstitious folk practice where an image of a saint was dipped or "drowned" in water to compel the saint to bring rain or perform a miracle.</note>. For, as **Saint Thomas [Aquinas]** says in the *Summa Theologica* (II-II, question 99, article 1): Sacrilege is the violation of a sacred thing—that is, the harming of a sacred thing—and he proves it thus: something is called "sacred" because it is ordained for divine worship. Just as a thing acquires the quality of "good" because it is directed toward a good end, so too something is made into a certain divine thing by the fact that it is set apart for the worship of God. And thus a certain reverence is owed to it, which is ultimately directed toward God; and therefore, everything that involves irreverence toward sacred things involves an injury to God, and has the character of **sacrilege** <term>sacrilegium: literally "the stealing of sacred things," but used broadly in theology to mean any disrespectful treatment of things dedicated to God</term>. These are his words. 

But that such a submersion of an image is sacrilege is proven by the same author in article 3 [of the same question], where he posits that the types of sacrilege are distinguished according to the sacred things involved, and that sacrilege has various degrees according to the differences between sacred things, places, and persons. For a sacrilege is more serious to the degree that the sacred thing against which the sin is committed possesses greater holiness. Among sacred things, however, the highest place is held by the **sacraments** <term>sacramenta: the primary ritual channels of grace in the Church, such as Baptism or the Eucharist</term>, by which man is sanctified, the foremost of which is the sacrament of the Eucharist—

It establishes a hierarchy of sacredness, noting that the gravity of sacrilege depends on the holiness of the object violated.</summary>

In this way, the fitting punishment for a sacrilegious person—who brings injury upon sacred things—is excommunication, through which he is barred from those very sacred things. Since punishments are inflicted as a kind of medicine, so that men, terrified by them, may desist from sin, a sacrilegious person who does not revere sacred things does not seem to be sufficiently restrained from sin simply by having sacred things forbidden to him, as he does not care for them. Therefore, according to human laws, the death penalty <term>pœna capitalis: the ultimate civil punishment, usually execution</term> is applied; however, according to the statutes of the Church, which do not inflict physical death, a monetary fine is applied, so that at least by temporal <note>earthly or financial</note> punishments, men may be called back from their sacrileges.

# THAT THOSE WHO SUBMERGE
## *images and relics are tempting God,*
## *and what it means to tempt God.*

From this it is clear that everyone who tempts God either is ignorant of God or doubts some perfection of His, which is always a sin. 

We take a test regarding someone through words and deeds. Through words, indeed, so that we may test whether He knows what we seek, or is able, or is willing to fulfill it. Through deeds, however, when by those things which we do, we explore another’s prudence, or will, or power.

At other times, however, it is done "interpretatively"—that is, when even if one does not intend to take a test, they nevertheless do or say that which seems directed toward nothing else but taking a test. And just as the perfection of a good will makes good men equal to the angelic spirits, so too does the perversity of the impious render them similar to demons. Wherefore, the more that evil and perverse men are depraved by the malice of their own will, the more they become similar to demons in their **disposition** <term>affectu: the internal state or "leaning" of the soul toward certain desires</term>. 

Indeed, through this similarity of character, a familiarity of friendship is introduced, from which a mutual confidence is gradually generated. Therefore, if any command over demons appears to exist for depraved men, it arises from the greatness of their depravity—specifically when their internal disposition is depraved to such an extent that, through their own **reprobate** <note>original: "reproba." ## Treatise on the Reprobate and Sorcerers

[Demons] concur with all **reprobate** <term>reprobi: in theology, those who are rejected by God and destined for damnation because of their persistent sin</term> and evil men in this way, but only with those with whom they have entered into treaties through some mediating pact, such as the **wicked women** <note>original: "maleficæ mulieres." While literally "evil-doing women," this is the standard Latin term for "witches" in this period.</note> who have pledged homage to the devil, and those invokers of demons whom the common people call **necromancers** <term>necromanticos: literally "corpse-diviners," but used here as a general term for sorcerers who summon spirits</term> in ordinary speech. There are two types of men who can lawfully command demons.

The first indeed is of those men who, beloved by God through the merit of holiness, have received from Him the power to trample the head of the **ancient serpent** <note>A common biblical metaphor for Satan, referencing the serpent in the Garden of Eden and the promise in Genesis 3:15.</note>, such as were the Apostles and their followers and disciples in the primitive Church, concerning whom the Lord speaks in the **Holy Gospel**: *In my name they shall cast out demons, and they shall take up serpents.* <note>original: "In nomine meo dæmonia eijcient, & quia serpentes tollent." Trithemius is quoting Mark 16:17-18.</note>

The second type, however, is of those men to whom it is granted by reason of their rank in the Church of God to drive out demons from the bodies of men through the power of the ministry they have received. And this ministry is entrusted to **exorcists** in the Church of God, specifically when they are ordained by a **bishop** <note>original: "pontifice." In an ecclesiastical context, this refers to a high-ranking prelate, usually a bishop, who has the authority to ordain.</note>.

On the other hand, there are two types of men who *desire* to command demons; the wicked conditions [of their pacts] show how unlawfully they presume to do so.

# ON THE POWER
## Of Witches.

From where does such great power come to witches, through which they are able to perform so many various and wonderful things even in a single hour—things of a quality or scale that no good man could accomplish in his entire life?

<summary>Trithemius argues that while modern men lack the holiness of the early saints required to command spirits, witches derive an alarming, rapid power from their pacts with demons. He contrasts the slow, merit-based miracles of the godly with the immediate, destructive works of sorcery.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the introductory chapter of the treatise. The previous page ended with the question: "From where does such great power come to witches?" This page provides the theological answer, asserting that all power ultimately originates from God.</meta>

->Page 464<-

->Treatise on the power of Witches<-

If we wish to answer this question briefly, we must necessarily say that all power is from the Lord God, without whom no creature can do anything. For Christ says in the Holy Gospel:

> Without me you can do nothing. <note>original: "Sine me nihil potestis facere"; a reference to the Gospel of John 15:5</note>

From this it is manifest that all power of doing anything is granted to men by the Lord God and from nowhere else, whether men work good or evil. On this point, the most holy Prelate **Augustine** says:

> The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and motions, and nothing happens visibly in this most ample and immense Republic of the whole creation which is not either commanded or permitted from the interior, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments. <note>Augustine's *De Trinitate*, Book III, Chapter 4. Trithemius uses the term "Republic" to describe the ordered structure of the universe.</note>

Therefore, it is not to be doubted, Caesar <note>Addressing Emperor Maximilian I, to whom this work is dedicated</note>, that the power of those witches—in which they produce wonderful and horrific effects with the cooperation of demons—is granted by the Lord God, whose will no one can resist, and without whose influence no man can even move his hand. For the holy Doctors conclude that neither demons nor witches can do anything at all, whether to harm a human or a beast, unless the almighty God wills it,

<summary>Trithemius argues that the power utilized by witches and demons is not independent, but is ultimately granted or permitted by God, as nothing in the universe occurs without Divine will or permission.</summary>

# Of Master Johannes Trithemius

...wills, consents, and grants the power, so that they may do what they have already decreed with their perverse will. Unless God consents and wills it, no creature can do anything; otherwise, if something could happen without Him willing and consenting, it would necessarily follow that God is weak, unable to prohibit what He was forced to permit against His will.

But because every human, insofar as they are a creature, depends on God, they can do nothing without the will of Him from whom they have both the *willing* and the *ability*. Therefore, whatever **witches** <note>original: "maleficæ"; specifically referring to those who perform harmful magic</note> do happens by God’s permission, without whose will they can do nothing, because they would obtain the power to do what they want neither from themselves nor from **demons** <note>original: "dæmonibus"</note>, unless God granted it.

Therefore, all power is from the Lord God, in whom all things both are and move <note>A paraphrase of Acts 17:28: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being."</note>, as in the first cause of all things; since from Him from whom we received **free will** <note>original: "libertatem arbitrij"</note>, we also have the ability to do what we desire.

But since the intellect of witches is greatly confused, they do not perform the evils they do by human skill, but by the **cooperation of demons**: whom nature has made subtle and long experience has made swift in producing wonders. This kind of witch differs greatly at times from the others, because while the others make a person sick through sorcery, these women promise to cure them. But because they generally repel one sorcery with another sorcery, the Church forbids any Christian from approaching them. ### Treatise on Divine Permission.

The response we gave to **Your Majesty, O Caesar**, is by no means absurd, for it in no way detracts from divine goodness that He permits evils to occur for a most just reason; indeed, it would rather be a detriment to His goodness if He did not permit evils to happen in this present world. For truly, if He did not permit evils to be done, then man would be unable to sin; he would certainly be **impeccable** <note>original: "impeccabilis"; the theological state of being unable to sin</note>, which is not suited to his nature, to which the **Creator** of all gave **free will** <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity of the soul to choose between good and evil, a central concept in Western theology</term> from the beginning. 

For since man is a creature and not the **Creator**, he is necessarily as capable of turning toward evil as toward good; his very existence depends upon the supreme **Artisan** <note>original: "opifice"; a term often used to describe God as the master craftsman of the universe</note> of all creatures, just as every effect depends upon the cause of its being. To create, however, belongs to God alone, who is incorruptible and eternal; whereas everything corruptible necessarily fails, yet is preserved by the goodness of the **Creator** so long as it does not lose the influence of its cause. 

Therefore, it was neither possible nor fitting that man, by the condition of his nature, should be created **impeccable**; this is a state enjoyed naturally only by God, the **Artisan** of all things, who is **unchangeable** <term>incommutabilis: constant and not subject to change or fluctuation</term> and eternal. Whenever it is granted to a man that he seems unable to sin, his **freedom of will** is not taken away, nor is the possibility [of sinning] simply removed; rather, the will is confirmed in goodness. And how oft-
<note>The catchword "enscun-" suggests the following page begins with "enscumque," completing the word "quotienscumque," meaning "howsoever often."</note>

<summary>Trithemius argues that God permits evil because man was created with free will, and to be truly human is to be capable of choosing either good or evil. He asserts that only God is naturally incapable of sin, and for God to force man to be "impeccable" would be a violation of the nature God gave him.</summary>

# Dr. Johannes Trithemius.

For **Scripture** says: *God created man from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel* <note>original: "Deus ab initio creauit hominem & reliquit eum in manu confilij ſui"; a citation of Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 15:14</note>. For, properly speaking, it is not possible for a mortal man, conceived in **original displeasure** <note>original: "originali diſplicentia"; a reference to the inherited state of original sin</note>, to possess both **free will** and the inability to commit sin. 

For the most holy prelate **Augustine** says: *The first freedom of the will was to be able to sin; the final freedom, in glory, will be much greater: not being able to sin* <note>A famous distinction made by St. Augustine of Hippo in "The City of God," Book 22</note>. Therefore, if man were unable to sin, he would not have mastery over his own will. For this reason, although **Almighty God** does not will sin, He nevertheless justly permits men to sin and to do evil; this is so that, while the freedom of choice remains, the virtue of a good work may receive its merit, and voluntary wickedness may receive the penalty for the evil it has done. For no one does good or sins against his will. 

Justly, therefore, does Almighty God permit men to sin and do evil, since He granted them **freedom of choice** <term>libertatem arbitrij: the theological concept that humans have the power to choose between different courses of action without necessity or fate</term> from the beginning. There are, however, many reasons assigned by the **Holy Doctors** <note>the authoritative early theologians of the Church</note> long ago as to why the Almighty permits such great **wicked deeds** <term>maleficia: in this context, the term specifically refers to harmful magic or "witchcraft" performed with demonic help</term> to occur through the cooperation of **demons**; we shall briefly mention these in their necessary order.

The first reason is that the excellence of divine power may be manifested, for He alone is **unchanging**, and is far above every station. Every creature, however, is subject to change, and has no comparison to the unchanging Creator. Hence, it is read in the Book of **Numbers**: *God is not like man that He should lie, nor like the son of man that He should be changed* <note>original: "Non eſt Deus quaſi homo vt mentia-tur, nec vt filius hominis vt mutetur"; referencing Numbers 23:19</note>. In **Isaiah** <note>The text attributes this to Isaiah, though the phrase "God is faithful and without iniquity, just and right" is found in Deuteronomy 32:4</note> it is also said: *God is faithful and without iniquity, just and upright.* In the book of **Tobit** it is also written: *You are just, O Lord, and all your judgments are true, and all your ways are mercy, truth, and judgment* <note>original: "Iuſtus es Domine, & o-mnia iudicia tua vera ſunt, & oēs viæ tuæ miſericordia, veritas & iudicium"; referencing Tobit 3:2</note>. And in the book of Saint **Job** we read: *Far be it from God to do wickedness, and from the Almighty to do iniquity. For He renders to man his work, and according to the ways of each He will restore to them* <note>original: "Abſit à Deo impie-tas, & ab omnipotente iniquitas. Opus e-nim hominis reddit ei, & iuxta vias ſingu-lorum reſtituet eis"; referencing Job 34:10-11</note>. Therefore, every person who rightly understands their own ignorance and weakness clearly recognizes how they are as nothing compared to their Creator. For God justly permits man to sin, so that both the **freedom of choice** <term>libertas arbitrij: the theological concept that humans have the power to choose their own actions</term> may be maintained, and the excellence of the great God may become known to men. 

The second reason is that the inscrutable wisdom of God may become known to mortals, which knows how to draw good out of our evils, since the sin of one becomes the **merit** <term>meritum: a work or state of being that is worthy of spiritual reward or divine grace</term> of another for the increase of virtue. For if He did not permit evil to be done, who among [ourselves]...

The third cause is that the Almighty permits evil deeds to take place so that He may manifest His most merciful goodness toward those who have sinned and performed penance <term>penance: the act of atonement or repentance for sin</term>, which He could in no way show if He did not permit the creature to sin. The fifth reason is the dignity of the human condition; for if God did not permit man to sin, he would seem lower than the beasts, which, with no force compelling them, use the movements of nature freely. ### Treatise on Divine Permission

<page-num>484</page-num>

[...lib]erty <note>original: "libertas," completing the word from the previous page</note> is manifest, nor [can the devil compel] a man whose will is however much depraved. The will is indeed free, but its power is limited by certain and necessary bounds. For if demons were able to do all that they wish, nothing in human affairs would remain safe, but they would overthrow everything.

The history of Saint Job clearly demonstrates this bound power of demons through an example; Satan did not dare to tempt him any further than had been permitted to him by divine dispensation. <note>original: "dispensatione divina." In theology, this refers to God's ordered plan or management of the world.</note> For no one in the present world, no matter how just or strong, could resist the fury of demons if they were always able to use the free power of harming as they pleased.

Before the Lord’s Passion <note>original: "dominicam passionem." The suffering and death of Jesus.</note>, they exercised a greater freedom of power than they did afterward; but since Christ tasted death for us on the altar of the cross, their power has been greatly diminished from that time forward. As the Savior says in the Gospel: *Now the prince of this world shall be cast out.* <note>Quoting John 12:31. "Prince of this world" was a common title for the devil in the Middle Ages.</note>

Indeed, the humility of Christ and the perseverance of the saints have greatly restrained the audacity of the demons, so that they may rightly be called **inciters** of evils, but by no means **impellers**. <term>inciters vs. impellers: Trithemius distinguishes between suggesting a sin (inciting) and forcing a person to act (impelling). He argues demons can tempt but cannot override human free will.</term> The devil would not grow strong against us if he did not receive strength from our sins. Hence Scripture warns us, saying: *Resist the devil and he will flee from you.* <note>Quoting James 4:7.</note>

<summary>This page argues that God strictly limits demonic power to protect humanity, noting that while demons can tempt humans, they cannot force them to sin. It emphasizes that the devil's power was significantly weakened following the crucifixion of Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conclusion of the previous argument regarding the limits of demonic power and the freedom of the human will. It transitions from the general nature of demonic will to the specific, troubling question of why God allows the faithful to suffer from witchcraft.</meta>

# D. Johannes Trithemius

...to you. And again: *Do not give place to the Devil.* <note>Quoting Ephesians 4:27. This serves as a warning that while the devil's power is limited, human choices can "open the door" to his influence.</note> Therefore, concluding this discourse regarding the understanding of the proposed question—why **GOD** permits so many evil acts <note>original: "maleficia." In this context, the term specifically refers to harmful magic or "witchcraft" intended to cause injury.</note> to occur—I believe the reasons have been made sufficiently manifest. For even if the will of demons is always wicked, their power can nevertheless never be unjust; because while they possess the desire to do evil from their own free choice <term>free choice: "arbitrio," the faculty of the soul to choose its own direction, though here directed toward evil.</term>, they possess the ability to actually perform that evil only from God.

And these things have been said insofar as they pertain to those who perform evil deeds. But why does almighty God permit demons to harm people by means of **witches** <note>original: "maleficarum." Trithemius uses the feminine form here, which was standard in the demonological treatises of the late 15th and early 16th centuries.</note>, who have been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity and faithfully believe in His only-begotten son, our Lord Jesus Christ? 

For if they were only able to harm the wicked, the perverse, and the faithless in their bodies and possessions, but were restrained from approaching or harming the good and the faithful, the judgment of [divine] permission would rightly seem just. But as it stands, the good and innocent are more frequently weakened by the witchcraft of demons, and sometimes even deprived of life—to say nothing of the loss of temporal goods <note>Temporal goods refers to physical property, money, or health, as opposed to spiritual or eternal treasures.</note> which those bewitched so often suffer—it becomes a point of doubt <note>original: "scrupulum." Literally a "small sharp stone" in one's shoe; metaphorically, a source of moral or intellectual anxiety or hesitation.</note> for many why the Almighty permits these things, He who permits nothing unjustly.

### Treatise on Divine Permission

Regarding this proposed question, which I have received from nowhere else but the ancient and Catholic Doctors <note>Referring to the "Fathers of the Church," such as Augustine or Jerome, whose writings formed the basis of medieval theology.</note>, I will set out the necessary reasons in order as briefly as I am able. 

And indeed, the first reason is the testing of the faith of Christians and the trial of their integrity, so that those scourged by the evil deeds <note>original: "maleficijs." In this context, it specifically refers to harm caused by demons or witchcraft.</note> of demons may learn, through the sufferings of the flesh, what faith and love they have toward God in the secret depths of their minds. It is not difficult to be long-suffering in prosperity, but to wait for help from the Savior of the faithful with humble patience in adversity is not the mark of the weak <note>original: "mollium," literally "soft," used here to describe those with a fragile or shallow faith.</note>, but of the strong and truly faithful Christians. 

The most holy **Job** learned in his tribulation how much constancy of faith he had in God—he who previously, in a state of tranquility, had guarded his piety without the arrows of temptation. From this, it must also be noted that those whom the evil deeds of demons or men have made sick in any way, who—in order to recover their health—either approach or consult any **sorcerers** and **enchanters** <note>original: "maleficos & incantatores."</note>, whether by themselves or through others, act against the commands of God and the Church. They possess neither true faith in God nor love. For they prefer the health of their dying flesh over God, and they seek salvation not from Christ, but from the devil and his minister. For they prefer...

O most holy **Caesar** <note>Addressing the Holy Roman Emperor, most likely Maximilian I, whom Trithemius advised on matters of theology and the occult.</note>, men of corrupt minds and rejected in their faith should not be tolerated among Christians—those who "cure" the victims of witchcraft <term>maleficiatos</term> <note>Literally "the bewitched"; those believed to be suffering from a curse or demonic affliction.</note> through further acts of witchcraft; those who reveal thefts and adulteries through the service of demons; and those who predict the future by gazing into stones or mirrors <note>A practice known as scrying or catoptromancy, common in both folk magic and "high" ritual magic of the period.</note>. 

I pray you do not listen to those who, ignorant of divine laws, believe such ministers of demons are useful to your empire because they know how to undo one curse with another <note>original: "maleficio... maleficia dissoluere." Trithemius is arguing against "counter-magic," stating that using magic to break a curse is still a sin.</note>. For such ruinous "healing" of the body brings about the death of the soul; it causes men to turn away from God, the creator of all, and to cling to the wicked, apostate demons, with whom they will be damned forever after death.

### Treatise on Divine Permission

...so that their patience, **tested** in tribulation, may merit a more worthy crown of glory in heaven. For as the holy **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian whose writings on the nature of evil and free will heavily influenced medieval thought.</note> says: 

> A man is unknown to himself regarding what he can bear and what he cannot; sometimes he fears he cannot do what he actually can. When temptation approaches like a sort of interrogator, a man is discovered by himself—he who, previously hidden, did not know himself.

The divine **Chief Apostle Peter** <note>original: "Archiapostolus Petrus." Trithemius refers to the biblical account where Peter boasted of his loyalty but denied Christ three times when tested by the threat of arrest.</note>, before temptation came upon him, was hidden both from himself and from others as to how reckless and weak he was; but when that temptation arrived, the weakness that had been hidden appeared. Therefore, the greatest proof of a man is temptation, as the **Holy Scripture** <note>The following quote is from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 27:5.</note> testifies: 

> The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests just men.

Patience is easy in prosperity, because no adversities strike the mind. 

> Many, however, are the **tribulations** <term>tribulationes</term> <note>From the Latin "tribulum" (a threshing sledge). In a theological sense, it refers to the "threshing" of the soul to separate the wheat of virtue from the chaff of sin.</note> of the just, but from them all our Lord Jesus Christ will deliver them.

The **third reason** for divine permission is the **guarding of humility**, so that the faithful and just man may always fear God and never presume upon his own strength or righteousness. Regarding the rejected, the Scripture says: 

> They are not in the labor of men, and they shall not be scourged with other men. Therefore pride has held them fast; they are covered with their iniquity and their impiety.

### Master Johannes Trithemius

...their iniquity has come forth as if from fatness. <note>original: "prodijt quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum." This is a citation of Psalm 73:7, suggesting that sin and injustice thrive in a state of excessive luxury and ease where the soul is "fattened" by prosperity.</note>

Indeed, **tribulation** has made many humble whom favorable circumstances would have rendered arrogant. Finally, the fearful imagination of **sorcery** <term>maleficia</term> <note>Literally "evil-doings," this term specifically refers to harmful magic or "witchcraft" believed to be performed through the aid of demons. The **fourth reason** is so that a distinction between the good and the bad might be maintained. For the Scripture says regarding good men and those beloved by God in the **Acts of the Apostles**:

> All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution. <note>2 Timothy 3:12.</note>

The most wise King **Solomon** also says in the Book of **Proverbs**: 

> Whom the Lord loves, He corrects, and He takes pleasure in him as a father does in a son. <note>Proverbs 3:12.</note>

It is an exceedingly glorious thing for a Christian to endure patiently for the love of God...

# Treatise on Divine Permission

...adversities, whether they are brought upon them by evil men or by demons. For power is given to the devil and his ministers to harm good and just men—not for their confusion, as sinners think, but rather for the greatest and most certain consolation of the soul. 

Indeed, when a just man lives well, he harms no one, offends no one, and does no one an injury. He loves his God with all his heart, fears and venerates Him, and keeps His commandments with all diligence. Nevertheless, he is troubled by **evildoers** <term>maleficis</term> <note>original: "maleficis." While it can mean "wrongdoers" generally, in this context Trithemius refers specifically to those practicing harmful magic or sorcery through demonic aid.</note>, whether in his **body**, his **possessions**, or in both. Truly, that man is blessed, because when he has been tested, he will receive the **crown of life** <note>original: "coronam vitae." A reference to James 1:12: "Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life."</note> which God has promised to those who love Him. 

Whoever lives rightly in the unity of the faith of the **Catholic Church** of Christians, and patiently tolerates the evils he receives in this world for the love of God, possesses a certain sign that he perseveres in God’s grace unto salvation. 

On the other hand, regarding the wicked and the reprobate, we read this written in Scripture: 

> Why do the impious live? They are lifted up and comforted with riches. Their houses are secure and peaceful, and the **rod of God** <note>original: "virga Dei." Referring to divine discipline or punishment. The absence of this "rod" suggests God has abandoned the wicked to their own desires.</note> is not upon them; they spend their days in good things, and in a moment they descend into hell. <note>This is a quotation from the Book of Job 21:7-13.</note>

For it is a manifest sign of damnation if you live badly here in sins and vices contrary to God, yet remain in **good fortune**...

The **fifth reason** why the Almighty permits good and just men to be troubled by the wicked and the reprobate is for the complete **purification** <term>purgationem</term> of the mind. For as Scripture says: *There is no just man on earth who does good and does not sin* <note>original: "Non est homo iustus in terra qui faciat bonum & non peccet." Out of mercy, He therefore commutes eternal punishment into temporal punishment for those who repent; it is necessary that they suffer this either in this world or after death in **purgatory**. 

Truly, because the torments of purgatory are horrendous and most grave, the merciful God is accustomed to purify the penitents whom He loves in this life in various ways, through the hardships of diverse tribulations in the body and in their worldly affairs. Indeed, the **evil deeds** <term>maleficia</term> <note>original: "maleficia." In the works of Trithemius, this specifically refers to harmful acts of sorcery or magic performed with demonic aid.</note> of the wicked benefit good and just men as a remedy, but lead to damnation for those who inflict them.

This describes a person who is the victim of a "maleficium," or a harmful curse/spell.</note> through the incursions of demons may be called back to repentance, and may resolve in his heart upon a necessary amendment of his life. ### Treatise on Divine Permission

...[God] sends vengeance, but waits until the predetermined time for our improvement. If, however, we neglect to perform **penance** <term>poenitentia</term>, the **avenger of evils** <term>vindex malorum</term> comes to us when we do not expect it; and we who, in times of tranquility, despised recognizing our sinful selves through penance, will finally recognize them, too late, in times of tribulation. Hence the holy **Prophet** <term>Propheta</term> <note>Referring to King David as the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> speaks in the person of God, saying:

> If his children forsake my law, and do not walk in my judgments, and if they do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with stripes; but I will not scatter my mercy from them, nor will I do harm in my truth. <note>original: "Si dereliquerint filij eius legem meam..." A quotation from Psalm 89:31–34 (Psalm 88 in the Vulgate numbering).</note>

The **seventh reason** why Almighty God permits the **evil deeds of demons** <term>maleficia daemonum</term> <note>original: "maleficia." This refers specifically to harmful sorcery or magical injuries believed to be facilitated by demons.</note> to prevail over the good and the innocent is so that an excessively indulgent opportunity for sinning might be cut off from them. For there are many poor and infirm people who are pleasing to God—good, devoted, and humble—whom **poverty** <term>inopia</term> and **bodily illness** <term>aegritudo corporis</term> preserve in the love of God; yet if these same people were wealthy and raised up by honors, they would quickly slide down from their purpose of holiness into the depths of vice. It is not beneficial for the **salvation** <term>salus</term> of everyone to possess honors and **wealth** <term>divitiae</term> along with health, nor does a longer life always make a man...

# From the Works of Johannes Trithemius

...better. Therefore, Almighty God, wishing to show His mercy toward those He has chosen, permits the good, the just, and the innocent to be subjected to various calamities. And sometimes through **demons** <term>daemones</term>, sometimes through evil men, and sometimes by various other modes and means, He takes away riches and honors from such people, knowing beforehand that they would have used them poorly; He does this so that they might preserve humility in poverty and lowliness—a humility they would never have maintained if they had been situated in wealth and high status.

He also frequently permits them to fall into many great **illnesses** <term>aegritudines</term>, because for them, the joyful health of the flesh would have brought about a profound sickness of the mind. Finally, He permits some to be driven to death by **sorcery** <term>maleficium</term> <note>original: "maleficio." Refers to harmful magic used to cause physical harm or death, often believed to be the result of a pact with demons.</note>, so that their freedom to sin—which they would have abused had they been permitted to live longer—might be cut off. Hence, regarding the just man, **Scripture** says:

> He was snatched away, lest wickedness should alter his understanding, or lest deceit should beguile his soul. <note>original: "Raptus est ne malitia mutaret intellectum eius..." A quotation from the Book of Wisdom 4:11.</note>

The **eighth reason** for divine permission is so that people might venerate the **Sacraments of the Church** <term>Sacramenta Ecclesiae</term>, which possess great power against all the **sorceries of evil spirits** <term>maleficia malignorum spirituum</term>. For a person is rarely harmed by the sorceries of demons if they venerate the Sacraments and **rites of the Catholic Church** <term>ritus Ecclesiae Catholicae</term> with due honor. Indeed, we have often heard from the very **confessions of witches** <term>confessione maleficarum</term> <note>The author refers here to the testimony obtained during trials or inquisitions of those accused of practicing harmful magic.</note>...

# ON SORCERY AND SORCERERS,
## testimonies from Holy Scripture and certain Church Fathers.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial letter 'G' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or biblical figure, within an ornate border.</image-desc> GALATIANS 5. *The works of the flesh are obvious, which are these: adultery, sexual immorality, etc., **sorcery** <term>veneficium</term> <note>original: φαρμακεία (pharmakeia). > *For whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord, and because of these abominations the Lord your God is driving them out before you.* <note>The text cites Jeremiah 27, but this is actually a quotation of Deuteronomy 18:12. In the First Book of Samuel, chapter 28, Saul performed the duty of a good prince when he removed the **spiritists** <term>pythonissis</term> <note>original: *pythonissis*, referring to the "spirit of Pytho." ## Saint John Chrysostom

> If someone is a **Physician** <term>medicus</term> and gives a potion, it should be accepted; one should not inquire too curiously into what it is, but it should be held as something conducive to health. But if he is a **sorcerer** <term>veneficus</term> <note>original: *veneficus*, meaning one who uses "venenum" (poison or potions). In this context, it refers to a magical practitioner rather than a medical one.</note>, a **mage**, or an **enchanter**, not only should you not inquire into what he is, but even his voice must be fled from as if it were deadly. ***On Fate, Sermon 7.***

# St. Augustine

*Furthermore, against the magical arts—about which certain extremely unfortunate and extremely impious individuals are pleased to boast in the name of Demons—I shall cite the public light itself as a witness. > *I call the gods to witness, and you, dear sister, and your*
> *sweet head, that I am girded with magical arts against my will.* <note>A quotation from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (Book 4, lines 492-493), where Queen Dido speaks of her reluctant recourse to magic.</note>

> *And I have seen sown harvests transported elsewhere.* <note>From Virgil's *Eclogues* (8.99). It refers to the ancient superstition that a sorcerer could magically steal a neighbor's crops.</note>

<margin>Plato distinguishes two kinds of harmful sorcery.</margin> 
Plato, in the eleventh book of the *Laws* <note>Plato’s last and longest dialogue, where he outlines the legal code for an ideal city.</note>, has this to say: "For there are indeed two types of sorcery <term>pharmakeiai</term> <note>original: *φαρμακείαι*</note> among the human race, following a certain distinct distribution. For the one which we have just now explicitly mentioned, is that which naturally harms bodies by means of other bodies <note>i.e., physical poisons or drugs.</note>; the other is that which, through certain tricks, incantations, and so-called binding-spells <term>katadesesi</term> <note>original: *καταδέσεσι* — ancient Greek "curse tablets" or spells intended to "bind" a person's will or physical abilities.</note>, persuades those attempting to do harm that they have such power, and convinces others that they are being harmed above all else by those who are able to perform such sorcery."

A little later, advising that a double law should be established for this reason, he says: "Dividing the law concerning sorcery <term>pharmakeia</term> into two parts, according to whichever way one might attempt to use spells or drugs."

Afterward, having established the law concerning those who do harm by administering a drug <note>original: *pharmaco exhibito*</note>, he sets down the other law regarding incantations in these words: "But if someone appears to be doing harm by means of binding-spells, or conjurations, or incantations, or any such sorceries whatsoever: if he be a prophet or a diviner <term>teratoskopos</term> <note>original: *τερατοσκόπος* — literally a "watcher of wonders," a specialist in interpreting omens or supernatural signs.</note>, let him be put to death; but if he be convicted of sorcery without being a prophet, let the same penalty befall him as well." <note>Plato's text suggests that while the "prophet" is more dangerous because of their status, any person using these "spells" to harm others should face the law.</note> He most clearly demonstrates here...

<summary>Erastus uses Plato's "Laws" to argue that ancient tradition recognized two distinct types of sorcery: physical poisoning and psychological or ritualistic "binding" spells, both of which were punishable by law.</summary>
