<page-num>507</page-num>

### Thomas Erastus on Witches.

<margin><unclear>10</unclear></margin> Plato notes that in that ancient age, men used the term sorcery <term>pharmakeia</term> <note>original: *φαρμακεία*</note> to refer not only to the use of poisons <note>original: *veneficia*</note>, but to every species of incantation by which someone might attempt to harm a human being, a beast of burden, or crops (for Plato himself also doubted whether harm could actually be inflicted in that manner). Indeed, so as not to seem to speak only of "bindings," enticements, and charms <note>original: *ligaturis, illicio, & carminibus*</note>—for just a moment before he had mentioned wax images <note>In ancient "sympathetic magic," an image made of wax represented the victim; harming the image was believed to harm the person.</note> buried at crossroads or beneath a threshold—he adds that general clause: "or by any other incantation." Another point to be noted here in passing is that he uses the words "to practice magic," "to bewitch," "to drug," and "to practice sorcery" <note>original: *μαγεύω, γοητεύω, φαρμάττω, φαρμακεύω*</note> to signify the same thing. Thus, in this passage, the terms sorcery, trickery, a magic spell, an invocation, a binding-spell, and an incantation <note>original: *φαρμακεία, μαγγανεία, μάγγανυμα, ἐπαγωγή, καταδεσμός, ἐπωδή*</note> all mean the same thing.

**FURTERIUS.** Do you have other witnesses besides these?

<margin>Aristotle uses the name "pharmakeia" for an incantation.</margin> 

**ERASTUS.** Aristotle also used the name sorcery <term>pharmakeia</term> in this way in the sixth book of his *History of Animals*, chapter eighteen, and in the ninth book, chapter seventeen. ### Thomas Erastus on Witches.

In chapter twenty-two, they are called **sorceresses** <term>pharmakides</term> <note>original: *φαρμακίδες*</note> when he writes: "for this reason, the sorceresses also seek and collect them." 

<margin>Aristophanes.</margin>
In the works of Aristophanes, who lived much earlier than Aristotle, we read of "Thessalian sorceresses" <note>original: *φαρμακίδες Θετταλαὶ*. Thessaly was a region in Greece renowned in the ancient world for its powerful witches and herbalists.</note>. It is a well-established fact that these women of Thessaly were incantatresses or witches. 

<margin>The commentator on Pindar.</margin>
The commentator on Pindar also writes that the women whom he calls **sorceresses** <note>original: *φαρμακίδας*</note> tie a bird called a **wryneck** <term>iynx</term> <note>original: *ἴυγγα*. In ancient Greek love magic, this bird was tied to a four-spoked wheel (called a *iynx-wheel*) and spun while incantations were recited to draw a lover toward the practitioner.</note> to a wheel and sing certain charms to bring back absent lovers. 

<margin>To practice sorcery means to enchant.</margin>
Furthermore, it hardly needs to be pointed out that the word **to practice sorcery** <term>pharmakeuein</term> <note>original: *φαρμακεύειν*</note> is very frequently used by authors to mean to enchant, or to perform illusions and deceptions. I will only add this: in the eighteenth chapter of Revelation, "sorcery" <term>pharmakeia</term> <note>original: *φαρμακείαν*</note> is used to mean superstition or deception, where it is written: "because by your sorcery all the nations were led astray" <note>original: *ὅτι ἐν φαρμακείᾳ σου ἐπλανήθησαν πάντα τὰ ἔθνη*; Revelation 18:23.</note>. Indeed, who does not know that the **Romanists** <note>A term used by Erastus, a Protestant reformer, to refer to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> have driven the nations mad not with physical poisons, but with superstitions and deceptions? From the beginning, I have also cautioned that all the Greek names used to describe various kinds of incantations or magic are frequently employed by authors to mean illusions, idols, deceptions, and so forth. This is because they considered almost everything attempted or performed by such people to be empty, futile, false, foolish, and deceptive.

**FURTERIUS. I understand why they called them sorceresses; now, explain why they called them Magi.** <note>The term *Magus* (plural *Magi*) originally referred to Persian priests but came to represent practitioners of magic in general.</note> **ERASTUS.**

# Thomas Erastus on Witches.

<margin>Concerning those who are and were formerly considered Magicians.</margin>
The Persian Magi were not only priests, but also **diviners** <note>original: *Diuinatores*; those who claim to predict the future or reveal hidden knowledge through supernatural means.</note> and performers of miracles. Therefore, at all times and in all places, those who appeared to have the knowledge or the ability to do things that cannot be achieved by **natural causes** <note>original: *naturalib. causis*. In the 16th century, "nature" was seen as a system of fixed laws; anything operating outside these laws was considered "supernatural" or "preternatural."</note> were considered Magicians. This is because these feats are greater and more wondrous than what can happen in a natural way. Since things that are not produced by natural causes cannot be attributed to either the known or the hidden powers of nature, they must be accomplished through the aid of a more powerful cause. Furthermore, only God and the angels—both good and bad—surpass the powers of nature. Therefore, such deeds must be attributed to the power of one of these.

<margin>Magicians use the works of the Demon.</margin>
Furthermore, it should be evident that Magicians rely on the help of neither God nor the good angels in their actions, because the things they attempt are utterly contrary to the order prescribed by God. It is required, therefore, that they use the service of **Cacodemons** <note>original: *Cacodemonum*. From the Greek *kakodaimōn*, literally meaning an "evil spirit" or "bad demon."</note>. But the demons do not assist just anyone; rather, they serve those to whom they have bound themselves by the force of a **pact** <note>original: *pactionis*. This refers to the "demonic pact," a central concept in early modern witchcraft trials where the witch was believed to have signed a formal contract with the Devil.</note>, whether manifest or hidden. For they do not assist everyone who pronounces those same words or uses the same objects in the same way. Indeed, a specific person, place, time, and method of acting is required, along with certain **symbols** <note>original: *characteres*. These were specific sigils or marks believed to have power in ritual magic.</note>, figures, and so on. From this, it is clearly seen that this power resides neither in the actions nor in the words. For if it were in the...

# Thomas Erastus on Witches.

<margin>Witches should be counted among Magicians.</margin>
...[whoever] professes to know secretly, or to be able to do, those things which cannot be accomplished by natural powers. Furthermore, it is absolutely certain that **witches** <note>original: *Sagæ*; Erastus uses this term to refer to those who claim occult wisdom or "keen perception" of hidden things.</note> believe they perform wonders through the favor of the **Devil**, and that they request such things from him by virtue of a **pact**. Therefore, it is also certain that they are rightly named as **magicians**.

<margin>A detestable species of Magic.</margin>
**FURIUS:** Do you propose many different types of this wicked Magic?

**ERASTUS:** An investigation into that does not belong here. Therefore, I will explain myself in just a few words. Some divide it into many parts, others into few. Elsewhere, as you know, we distinguished between **Divinatory** magic <note>original: *Diuinatricem*; the art of predicting the future or uncovering hidden knowledge through signs or spirits.</note> and **Operative** magic. For although almost all magicians claim to have knowledge of both categories, some focus more on one, and some on the other. And since witches are not so much occupied with foretelling the future, but are rather focused on "doing" or "acting," we place them instead among the **operative magicians** <note>original: *operatores Magos*; those who perform "works" or spells to cause physical effects, such as harming livestock or changing the weather.</note>—though we do not entirely exclude them from the company of the others.

Furthermore, the different categories or types of Operative Magic are usually defined by the tools and the methods of acting. But there is such confusion here that nothing certain or permanent can be established. Nor does any necessity compel us at this time to investigate this matter with excessive detail <note>original: *superstitiosè*; in this context, it means with an overly fastidious or obsessive attention to minor points.</note>.

**FURIUS:** I require nothing further on this; but I would rather hear why you call them **Lamiae**? <term>Lamiae: derived from a Greek myth of a child-devouring demon; in the Early Modern period, it became a common Latin term for "witches."</term>

**ERASTUS:** They are called **Lamiae** because of the simil—

<margin>What a **spell** is.</margin>
Furthermore, the ancients used the term **harmful spell** <term>carmen</term> <note>original Latin: *carmen*, meaning a song, poem, or ritual chant.</note>, and we ought to use it as well, to refer not only to a long chant but even to a curse or imprecation consisting of only one or two words. Of natural things, which are truly and simply such, there is no other author than **Nature**, which is the ordinary power of God bestowed upon things in creation itself. If Demons could produce these things by their own powers without the intervention of natural seeds <note>original: "naturalium seminum"; in the 16th century, this referred to the "seminal reasons" or hidden principles in nature that allow things to grow and develop.</note>, we would be forced to admit they are creators.

It is certain that a purging quality can be joined to astringent things, a healthy quality to unhealthy things, and conversely, a harmless quality to harmful things.

Finally, this too has clearly been seen: that some things are brought to birth and to proper maturity much earlier or later than their nature dictates. For who does not know that the **Egyptian Magi** did not fight against **Moses** with poisons or poisoned cups, but sought to evade his commands with **incantations** and **illusions**? Truly, these great men seem to have acted with great wisdom...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue on page 545, where Thomas Erastus is justifying the existence of specific laws against witchcraft. <page-num>546</page-num>
# Thomas Erastus on Witches.

It is well known that they <note>Referring to the witches/practitioners mentioned on the previous page</note> do not always, indeed not even frequently, see their wishes fulfilled. Yet, not without cause, the ancients enacted a specific law regarding them, by which they decreed that such practitioners were guilty of homicide. For indeed, Plato, in the 11th book of the *Laws*, judged as follows:

> Whenever one person harms another by means of potions <term>pharmakois <note>original Greek: φαρμακοῖς; the term refers to both medicinal drugs and poisonous or magical substances</note></term>, the fatal instances among them have already been discussed. But as for other types of harm—whenever someone intentionally harms another through drinks, or foods, or ointments—none of these has yet been defined. For there are two types of poisoning <term>pharmakeiai <note>original Greek: φαρμακεῖαι; the root for our word "pharmacy," but in this context, it covers both chemical poisoning and sorcery</note></term> among the human race that require a legal distinction. One is that which we just spoke of explicitly: harming bodies by means of other bodies according to the laws of nature. The other consists of sorceries, incantations, and binding spells <note>original Greek: μαγγανείαις καὶ ἐπωδαῖς, καὶ καταδέσεσι; "binding spells" refers to the practice of "tying" or "binding" a victim through a curse</note>, and so forth.

Plato here clearly affirms that the logic behind lethal poisons is not the same as that of enchanted potions. Therefore, distinct laws ought to be passed concerning them, since the manner of doing harm is not the same. For the former is natural, while the latter appeared even to the ancients to have risen above the limits of nature. 

**FURIUS:** <note>Erastus uses "FUR." as an abbreviation for an interlocutor in this dialogue</note> I submit to this reasoning, since I have nothing I can rightly oppose to it. You may therefore add whatever else you have to say.

<margin>
6.
Witches <note>original: "Striges"; classical screech-owl witches</note> practice a capital art. 
[Consulting] a prophet or a mage...
</margin>
**ERASTUS:** What of the fact that the practice of this art—or rather, this vanity—is a capital offense <note>a crime punishable by death</note>, even if it is practiced or sought after solely for the sake of pleasure or as a joke? What I am saying is clearly evident from the fact that God seriously commands that anyone who merely consults a fortune-teller <term>Ariolum <note>a soothsayer or diviner</note></term>, a mage, or a prophet...

Magicians are driven voluntarily by a certain insane pride of spirit, or moved by forbidden curiosity, to apply their minds to these arts; Witches, however, perform whatever they do because they have been persuaded by the devil. It is, moreover, far more serious to commit a crime out of one's own will and deliberation than to be led into it by certain enticements; therefore, they should not both suffer the same punishment. 

Consider the example of two murderers: one kills a man after debating the matter within himself, driven by a lust for doing evil; the other commits the same deed after being led by the persuasions of others. It is certain that the first has deserved the death penalty; the second we say is either excusable or should be punished with a far milder penalty, because the act of the former has an internal cause, while the latter's cause is external. Furthermore, the witches <note>original: *striges*; a term derived from ancient Roman folklore describing screech-owl-like creatures that fed on infants, used here to denote the specific "night-witch" archetype</note> of our time were not known to Moses. Therefore, he could not have included them within the definition of Magicians.

**ERASTUS.** 
<margin>Several types or modes of Magicians.</margin>

If only those Magicians are included under the name of "Magicians" who share every single characteristic, I will gladly grant that Witches cannot be counted among Magicians. For we have already demonstrated that they do many things differently. But in terms of wickedness, Witches surpass...

**ERASTUS:** But indeed, if a confession extorted by interrogations is not valid, then no (or certainly very few) thieves, traitors, or other criminals would ever be justly punished. For it is a rare thing for men to confess their committed crimes voluntarily. 

**FURIUS:** By the force of torments <note>original: *tormentorum*—the specific physical instruments or acts of torture used to extract information.</note>, some people certainly confess to what they never actually perpetrated. 

**ERASTUS:** But for that reason, by interrogations not...

<margin>Hidden crimes are eventually uncovered.</margin>

Therefore, you would despise a confession wrung out by torture in vain. As for a spontaneous confession, I would indeed strongly like to understand why it should not be valid. 

**FURIUS:** Because they either confess to things impossible to do, or to things that could indeed have happened but did not actually occur, or they did happen, but not by the hands of those confessing. 

**ERASTUS:** I believe you have forgotten what you undertook to prove: namely, that these women did not forge a pact with the Demon. The question now is not whether they are able to pull stars down from heaven, stir up storms, fly through the air, or penetrate through closed doors—but whether they have contracted a society, or a pact, or a friendship with the Evil Spirit <note>original: *Cacodemone*—a term derived from Greek meaning a malevolent spirit or "bad demon."</note>? 

<margin>To contract a society with the devil is not impossible.</margin>
Is this act impossible to do? I do not believe you believe that. Why then do you repeat those things, and strive to show that no covenant is struck with the Demon? It is both possible to do, and it has been done more often than I would wish.

...nor are they "Melancholic" <note>Referring to the 16th-century medical theory that an excess of "black bile" caused hallucinations or madness; the "Melancholy" defense was often used to argue that witches were mentally ill rather than evil.</note>, nor any more devoid of mind and reason (which my adversary repeatedly asserts) than other criminals: as has already been shown many times. Both their sluggish sex <note>A common 16th-century prejudice that women were intellectually "inert" and thus incapable of complex crime.</note> and their dull age prove that none of this is actually happening. **ERASTUS:** What kind of piety is this? To defend the opinion you have already formed in your mind, you seem ready to deny even that the sun shines at midday.

...they hand down accounts filled [with these things]. I ask you, do the things he recounts regarding parents and brothers in those books not bear a greater resemblance to fables than to the truth? I will pass over in silence the fact that those letters which contain certain transcriptions from the *Itinerary* <note>The *Itinerary of Saint Peter* was a popular but apocryphal account of the Apostle Peter's travels.</note> were, for this very reason, suspected by the ancients. As for what should be thought of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, there is no theologian today who does not know <note>By Erastus’s time, these "Constitutions" were widely recognized as 4th-century fabrications, not the work of the original Apostles.</note>. <margin>How the private parts are said to be taken away.</margin>

We commonly say that someone’s private parts <note>original: *pudenda*</note> have been "taken away" whenever they lose the use of them, whether this happens because of paralysis <note>original: *resolutionem*</note> or retraction. And we do not speak incorrectly in this way. For an eye is correctly called an eye only so long as it is an instrument of vision. When it is deprived of this use, it is no more an eye than a painted eye or a stone eye. Indeed, the instruments of the body—for whose sake each part was made—are defined by their function and power, as both Galen and Aristotle taught <note>Galen and Aristotle were the two primary authorities on biology and medicine in the 16th century; Erastus is using their logic to argue that a non-functional organ is effectively "gone."</note>. Suppose, then, that someone who is not insane thinks they are truly deprived of these limbs, even though it is not true. And suppose some witch <term>Saga: a traditional term for a wise woman or sorceress</term> had sexual relations with a demon only through a dream; is the sin equal in both cases? Or is there no...

of all which things most <term>witches</term> <note>original: *striges*. In this context, Erastus uses the term for those who have entered a voluntary pact with the Devil.</note> suffer nothing.
The examples which you have read cited from the holy books sufficiently
prove this, so that to pour out more words here would be to
do what has already been done. Next, the <term>possessed</term> <note>original: *obsessi*. In early modern theology, "the possessed" were seen as victims whose bodies were occupied by demons against their will, as opposed to witches who were seen as collaborators.</note> are not of sound
mind, or at least they cannot use it during the
time of their <term>paroxysms</term> <note>original: *paroxysmorū*. Violent fits or sudden attacks of symptoms, often associated with both medical epilepsy and demonic possession.</note>. For they are tortured by diseases so heavy
and bitter that during these flare-ups they do
not seem to be of sound mind. The opposite happens
in Witches, who enjoy good health
and show no sign of a damaged mind.
Furthermore, they do not speak in a <note>Speaking in unknown languages (xenoglossia) was considered a primary diagnostic sign of true demonic possession.</note> foreign tongue
at any time, as the possessed often do.
What of the fact that the possessed, when they have lucid intervals,
plead with groaning and the greatest pain
if they said or did anything wrongly,
stating they gave no consent to the demon
who used their tongues and limbs
against their own will? <term>Witches</term> <note>original: *Sagæ*. Another Latin term for witches, emphasizing their role as "wise women" or sorceresses.</note>, on the
other hand, are so far from showing themselves to repent of their crimes,
that they grieve most of all if they were unable to
complete what they desired to do.
Fifth, witches are accustomed to
boast of their expertise in marvelous things, and
some kind of knowledge of performing miracles:
of which the possessed claim nothing for themselves.
Nor do the possessed ever remember
any pact contracted with the devil:
nor were they ever delighted
by the presence of the Demon: but they ask
with their mouth and heart that it be as far
away from them as possible forever.

<summary>Erastus distinguishes witches from the demonically possessed by highlighting that witches act with sound mind, physical health, and personal intent, whereas the possessed are involuntary victims of fits and foreign tongues.</summary>

<keywords>Thomas Erastus, demonic possession, witchcraft, moral responsibility, legal sanity, paroxysms, demonic pacts, repentance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Erastus (ER) and Furius (FVR). Erastus is distinguishing between the "possessed" (who are unwilling victims of demons) and "witches" (who voluntarily cooperate with the Devil). On the previous page, he began listing differences: the possessed are tormented and often speak in tongues, whereas witches generally appear healthy and speak normally.</meta>

<page-num>603</page-num>
<header>Thomas Erastus on Witches <note>original: *Th. Erastus de Lamiis*</note></header>

...they seek help. Witches, on the other hand, rejoice to be in the presence of their <term>lovers</term> <note>original: *amasios*. This refers to the early modern belief in the "incubus," a demon that takes male form to have sexual relations with witches.</note>; they call out for them when they are absent, they urge them on when they linger, and they receive them with applause when they arrive. When interrogated, they all confess with one voice that they have entered into a pact. Finally, hardly any witches admit to being "possessed," whereas truly possessed people, in their moments of clarity, primarily grieve, mourn, and deplore this one thing above all else.

**FVR.** How could such great wickedness and such great impiety take hold of them, if the Devil did not possess their minds?

**ER.** I was speaking of the <term>possessed</term> <note>original: *obsessis*. From the Latin *obsidere* (to besiege), referring to those whose bodies are externally or internally controlled by a demon against their will.</note> in the way everyone is accustomed to speak according to the Holy Scriptures: namely, when Satan has occupied the body and governs, agitates, and <term>rides</term> <note>original: *equitat*. A common theological metaphor where the demon acts as a rider and the human body as the horse.</note> it according to his own will. When he besets the mind alone in order to drive it toward outrages, the person "possessed" in that way is not excused—unless you decide that all <term>wicked criminals</term> <note>original: *scelerosos*</note> ought to be acquitted.

**FVR.** I will say frankly what I think. When I first began to read the book, I thought there was something solid in it. Two things moved me to think so: First, that the man is exceptionally learned, as well as prudent and pious. Second, because I knew he had been asked by you that, if he decided to write anything against our view, he should provide it with stronger <term>arguments</term> <note>original: *argumentis*</note>. Therefore, I believed that, having weighed the matter most diligently and relying on better reasons, he had dared to attack our <term>opinion</term> <note>original: *sententiam*</note>. But the reality itself clearly shows that he has brought nothing new, but has merely repeated earlier points.

**ER.** That is how the matter stands. If it were true, which is claimed everywhere and almost exclusively in...

<summary>Erastus argues that witches are legally and morally responsible for their actions because they enjoy their bond with the Devil, unlike the possessed who suffer. Furius expresses disappointment that a certain author (likely Johann Weyer) has failed to provide new or solid arguments to the contrary.</summary>
<keywords>possession, pact with the devil, moral responsibility, incubus, legal excuse, Thomas Erastus, demonic influence</keywords>

--- Page 644 ---
<meta>This page concludes the argument from the previous page, where Erastus was debating the nature of demonic influence. He now addresses the psychological state of those accused of witchcraft and critiques the motives of those who defend them out of pity.</meta>

<page-num>604</page-num>
<header>Thomas Erastus on Witches <note>original: *Th. Erastus de Lamijs*</note></header>

He insists on this cause: that <term>witches</term> <note>original: *Lamias*. A term for female witches or sorceresses, often associated with the Roman myth of a child-eating demon.</note>, because their <term>imagination</term> <note>original: *phantasiam*. In early modern science, the *phantasia* was a physical faculty of the brain that processed and stored sensory images.</note> is occupied by false images, do not admit true ones (just as a mirror tinted with a specific color does not receive all colors; yet there is nevertheless a huge difference between a mirror and the imagination). We might probably think that something similar happened to this most distinguished and famous man <note>Erastus is likely referring to his intellectual opponent Johann Weyer, a physician who famously argued that many "witches" were merely mentally ill women.</note>. For because he was moved by pity for unhappy women, he deeply impressed this upon his imagination: that an injustice was being done to them. (And he is not entirely wrong: for many innocent women are killed because they were named by the guilty, and the guilty are tortured more cruelly than is right). Thereafter, he could not easily give space to true reasons. 

But while this can be affirmed to some extent regarding the sick and those suffering from <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: *melancholicis*. At the time, "melancholy" was seen as a physical ailment caused by an excess of black bile, often leading to hallucinations or delusions.</note>, it is absolutely true in the healthy. Whatever the case, you have rightly said that he has not now brought forward anything firmer or better; this would grieve me greatly if something more certain could be found. For I would rather die than err knowingly and deliberately in such a great matter, since such an error is not without the greatest <term>impiety</term> <note>original: *impietate*</note>. May the only-begotten and eternal Son of the eternal God the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, grant that we may all feel as one in Him, and, having set aside our passions, keep the eyes of our mind fixed upon the one truth. Amen. July 1st, in the year [15]77.

->*T H E  E N D*<-

<summary>In this concluding passage, Erastus argues that while some "witches" may be delusional or unjustly tortured, many are truly guilty, and he critiques the physician Johann Weyer for being blinded by pity. He ends with a prayer for unity and religious truth in the face of these difficult theological questions.</summary>

<keywords>Thomas Erastus, Johann Weyer, imagination, melancholy, judicial torture, legal justice, Christian unity, 1577</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as the colophon, or printer’s finishing statement, for the work by Thomas Erastus. The previous page concluded the textual argument regarding the mental state of those accused of witchcraft and the influence of "melancholy" on their imagination. This final page provides the publication details and the printer’s decorative emblem.</meta>

# PRINTED AT FRAN-
## kfurt am Main, at the shop of
## Nicolaus Bas-
## saeus.

<image-desc>The ornate woodcut printer's device of Nicolaus Bassaeus. An oval central frame depicts the nude female figure of Opportunity <note>original: *Occasio*. In Renaissance iconography, Opportunity is depicted as a woman balancing on a wheel to show instability, holding a razor to show she cuts through quickly.</note> balancing on a wheel amidst waves. She holds a razor in her right hand and a large, billowing piece of cloth as a sail in her left. In the background, a coastal city and a sailing ship are visible. The oval border contains the Latin motto "Opportunity has hair on her forehead, but behind she is bald" <note>original: *FRONTE CAPILLATA EST POST HAEC OCCASIO CALVA*. This proverb warns that one must seize an opportunity by the forelock as she approaches, because once she passes, there is no hair behind to grab hold of.</note>. The device is set within a rectangular frame of elaborate scrollwork and foliage, with two winged putti <note>Cherub-like figures common in Renaissance art.</note> reclining at the top.</image-desc>

## 1581.

<summary>This is the colophon page for Thomas Erastus's treatise on witches, identifying Nicolaus Bassaeus as the printer in Frankfurt am Main in 1581. It features the prominent "Occasio" printer's mark, symbolizing the fleeting nature of opportunity.</summary>
